Rhiannon goes in after him, takes hold of the same bowl, and is trapped beside him — and fort, bowl, and both prisoners vanish. Manawydan undoes the spell by patience. Sowing wheat, he watches three ripe fields stripped bare by mice on successive nights, and on the third he catches one slow, heavy mouse and condemns it to hang as a thief. A clerk, a priest, and a bishop come one after another to beg it off, each offering more than the last, and Manawydan names his price: Pryderi and Rhiannon released, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, and no vengeance taken. The mouse is the wife of Llwyd fab Cilcoed, transformed with all his household; Llwyd had laid the spell to avenge his friend Gwawl fab Clud. Pryderi comes home with the gate-hammer about his neck, and Rhiannon with the collars of asses about hers — the second humiliation she has worn like a queen, and the second she survives. Second Branch · Branwen ferch Llŷr: The Birds of Rhiannon Rhiannon never steps on stage in the Second Branch, but her birds do. When the seven survivors of the Irish war come back over the sea bearing the wounded head of Brân the Blessed, they feast at Harlech for seven years, and there come three birds — the Birds of Rhiannon, Adar Rhiannon — that begin to sing to them. Every other song seems unlovely beside it; and though the birds must be gazed at far out over the sea, their singing is as clear as if they sang in the hall. At Gwales in Penfro the company feasts on for eighty years with the uncorrupted head, in the presence of the birds' song, until the door toward Cornwall is opened and memory and sorrow return. Later Welsh tradition says of the Adar Rhiannon that their song wakes the dead and lulls the living to sleep — the music of a world that does not end. Syncretism: The great comparative debate pairs Rhiannon with Epona, the Gaulish horse-goddess whose dedications — more than two hundred inscriptions from Britain to the Balkans — make her the best-attested Celtic deity of the Roman west. A queenly rider whose whole story is bound to horses, whose name the handbooks reconstruct as 'Great Queen', looks very like an insular reflex of the mare-goddess; Mac Cana and others have argued the parallel, and Koch registers it as the standard comparison — but no inscription names Rhiannon or *Rīgantonā, and the identification remains typological, not epigraphic. The second frame is sovereignty: Mac Cana reads the First Branch against the Irish pattern in which the land's queen chooses and validates the king, so that Pwyll's marriage to Rhiannon is his investiture as much as his wedding. The third is Macha, the Irish sovereignty figure forced to race the king's horses: horse, humiliation, and queenship cluster around both women, and the handbooks have compared them for a century. None of these parallels is an identity; together they map the kind of goddess the Welsh prose is remembering. Cultural legacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Rhiannon out of the Welsh manuscripts and into the English-speaking world, and the Victorian Celtic revival made her one of the best-known figures of Welsh tradition. Evangeline Walton's twentieth-century retellings of the Four Branches kept her before modern readers, and in 1975 Fleetwood Mac's 'Rhiannon' — written by Stevie Nicks, who found the name in a novel and only afterwards learned it belonged to a Welsh goddess — made the name famous worldwide; the given name Rhiannon, already living in Wales, spread across the English-speaking world in the song's wake. In modern Druid and pagan practice she is honoured as a goddess of horses, sovereignty, and endurance under injustice, and scholars of the Mabinogi rank her among the most fully realized women in medieval European literature — a figure whose dignity the prose never once allows to slip. Extended meditation: Rhiannon cannot be caught because she has already decided where she is going. The fastest horses in Dyfed gallop themselves to exhaustion behind a rider who is barely trotting — and the moment she is asked, she stops, because stopping was always hers to give. That is the secret the First Branch teaches about power: the pace of a sovereign is not set by her pursuers. The rest of her story tests the lesson. Falsely accused, she does not rage or plead; she sits down by the horse-block and carries her guests, one by one, until the truth walks home on its own legs. Trapped in the enchantment, she endures the collars of asses and comes out still the Great Queen. Endurance, in her telling, is not passivity — it is the refusal to let an unjust sentence write your name. She waits, she carries, she outlasts; and the land is hers again. Original script note: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Rhiannon — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: rhiannon.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/rhiannon/ in the meantime.

title: Magic, Poetry, Trickery
text: Magic, Poetry, Trickery: The domain of Gwydion In the celtic tradition, Gwydion governed magic, craft, vengeance. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order. The Enchanted Swine: Disguised as a poet, Gwydion conjured illusory stallions, hounds, and shields to trade for Pryderi's otherworld pigs — the first swine in Wales — and started a war with a vanishing herd. Math's Wand: The wand that transformed Gwydion and Gilfaethwy into deer, boars, and wolves for three years — and that later struck Lleu from eagle back into man. The Flower-Maiden: With Math, Gwydion fashioned Blodeuwedd from the flowers of oak, broom, and meadowsweet — a wife made by craft for the man no earthly wife was allowed. The Eagle on the Oak: When Lleu was struck into eagle-shape, Gwydion followed a sow to the oak, sang three englynion to bring him down, and turned vengeance into restoration. Symbols: The magic wand — Math's wand of transformation — punishment, testing, and restoration carried in a single rod; Oak, broom, and meadowsweet — The three flowers from which Blodeuwedd was made by enchantment; The illusory horses and hounds — Gwydion's conjured wealth, real for a day and gone by morning — craft as currency; The eagle on the oak — Lleu wounded into bird-shape, rotting flesh feeding a sow beneath the tree; The sow — The beast Gwydion followed through the valley to find his foster-son; The shoemaker's disguise — The craft under which Gwydion tricked Arianrhod into naming her own son Gwydion fab Dôn is the enchanter of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, 'Math fab Mathonwy': nephew of Math the king of Gwynedd, brother of Gilfaethwy, and the foremost magician of medieval Welsh literature. He is poet, trickster, foster-father, and avenger in one figure — the man who makes illusions that pass for wealth, who pays for his crimes in animal skins, and who ends the tale as the careful hand that puts a broken world back into shape. Math fab Mathonwy: The War for the Swine King Math of Gwynedd could live only with his feet in the lap of a virgin, except in time of war, and the maiden Goewin held that office. When Gilfaethwy desired her, Gwydion devised the remedy: war. He went to Pryderi of Dyfed in the guise of a poet and asked for the swine — the hobeu, the first pigs ever brought to Wales, a gift from Arawn of Annwfn. Refused, he conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, and traded the apparitions for the herd. By the time Pryderi's glamour faded, Gwydion was gone, and Pryderi came north with an army. While Math marched to meet him, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin. At the peace-talks Pryderi demanded single combat, 'for it was because of me that the hosts came'; at Maenor Penard, the tale says, Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed went home under tribute. The victory is real and so is its cost: Gwydion's finest trick is also his crime, and the Fourth Branch never lets the two be separated. Math fab Mathonwy: The Punishment of the Brothers Math's justice is the strangest in the Mabinogi. He struck Gwydion and Gilfaethwy with his magic wand and turned them into a stag and a hind, and sent them into the wild for a year; when they returned with a fawn, he made them a boar and a sow for the second year, and a wolf and a she-wolf for the third. Each year their offspring — Hyddwn, Hychddwn Hir, and Bleiddwn — were sent to the court, baptized, and raised. After the third year Math struck them back into their own shapes: 'You have had punishment enough, and you have been greatly shamed.' The punishment is exact and even-handed — the brothers suffer in the flesh what they did, and when the debt is paid the king takes them back into honour. It is the Fourth Branch's doctrine of justice in miniature: transformation as sentence, restoration as mercy. Math fab Mathonwy: The Naming and Arming of Lleu When Gwydion proposed his sister Arianrhod as Math's new footholder, she stepped over the wand for the virginity test and dropped a yellow-haired boy — Dylan, who made for the sea — and 'something small' that Gwydion hid in a chest at the foot of his bed. From the chest came the boy who would be Lleu. Gwydion fostered him, and Arianrhod, shamed, laid three tynghedau upon him: he should have no name until she named him, no arms until she armed him, and no wife of any race then on earth. Gwydion undid the destinies by craft. Disguised as a shoemaker with the boy at his side, he came beneath Caer Arianrhod, and when Lleu flung a stone and knocked a wren's leg askew, Arianrhod cried that the fair one had struck it with a skilful hand — and so named him Lleu Llaw Gyffes. For the arms, Gwydion conjured a phantom fleet against the castle until Arianrhod herself armed the defenders. The magician wins not by force but by arranging the world so that his opponent speaks the words he needs. Math fab Mathonwy: The Flower-Maiden and the Eagle For the third tynged there was no earthly answer, so Gwydion and Math took their wands and made one: from the flowers of the oak, the broom, and the meadowsweet they fashioned the fairest woman anyone had seen, and named her Blodeuwedd, 'Flower-face'. She married Lleu — and betrayed him with Gronw Pebr of Penllyn, drawing from her husband the secret of how he could be killed, so that Gronw's spear struck him at the impossible meeting of conditions. Lleu flew off in the shape of an eagle, screaming. Gwydion searched Gwynedd and Powys until he followed a sow to an oak where rotten flesh and maggots fell to her snout, and in the top of the tree sat the eagle. He sang three englynion down the years of the bird's perches until Lleu came to his knee, then struck him with the wand back into human shape — skin and bone, a man to be nursed back with doctors and good care. The vengeance that followed was as crafted as the rescue: Blodeuwedd he would not kill, but turned into an owl, 'the shape hated by all the birds', renamed Blodeuwedd, 'Flower-face' become 'Owl'; and Gronw, standing where Lleu had stood, took Lleu's spear-cast through the slab at Llech Gronw and died. Maker of the woman, finder of the man, instrument of the sentence: the whole of Gwydion's domain is in this last movement. Kat Godeu: The Battle of the Trees Outside the Mabinogi, the Book of Taliesin preserves Gwydion's other great fame: Kat Godeu, 'The Battle of the Trees', in which he enchants the trees of the forest to march as an army against Arawn of Annwfn — alder at the front, oak in the thick of it. The poem's voice, Taliesin, boasts that he was there when Gwydion 'made the sally of the trees'. In the later tale-tradition around the poem, Gwydion also guesses the hidden name of the opponent's champion from the alder twigs in his hand — the same gift of naming-by-craft that the Fourth Branch shows in the wren scene. Whether the poem preserves older myth or learned fancy is debated, but its Gwydion is unmistakably the Mabinogi's: the magician whose weapons are other things' natures. Syncretism: Gwydion is the Welsh trickster-enchanter, and comparative scholarship has set him beside the other shape-changing cunning figures of Europe: [[loki|Loki]], whose disguises and bargains Gwydion's deceptions recall; [[hermes|Hermês]], the poet-thief of the Greek pantheon; and Óðinn in his sorcerer's aspect. Mac Cana treats him as one of the great magician-figures of the Celtic world, and the comparison holds at the level of motif — illusion, disguise, the hidden name, the shape-shifting punishment — not of borrowing. The deeper kinship is insular: Irish tradition is full of druidic shape-shifters, and Gwydion's transformations of and by Math belong to a shared Celtic idiom of magic as metamorphosis. Scholars have also long linked the Fourth Branch's otherworld material — Arawn's swine, the phantom fleet — to the mythology of [[manawydan|Manawydan]] and the First and Third Branches. Cultural legacy: Gwydion's afterlife runs from Welsh tradition into modern letters. Later Welsh usage named the Milky Way Caer Gwydion, 'Gwydion's fortress' — the enchanter's castle written across the night sky — and the antiquarian bards kept his tree-battle in the poetic canon. In the twentieth century he entered world literature twice over: Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967) rebuilt the Blodeuwedd tragedy as a haunting that repeats itself down the generations of a Welsh valley, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain gave young readers a Prince Gwydion fab Don, heir of Math, drawn directly from the Fourth Branch. Evangeline Walton's retellings of the Mabinogion made his punishment and restoration the moral hinge of her Fourth Branch volume. In scholarship he remains the standard exhibit of the Welsh magician: Ifor Williams's edition, Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi, and Koch's Celtic encyclopedia all treat the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose and Gwydion as its animating intelligence. Extended meditation: Gwydion is what a culture makes of cleverness when it refuses to call cleverness innocent. His illusions win a war and buy a rape; the tale answers by putting him, for three years, into the bodies of beasts, one year for each shape of the debt. But the same hands that tricked a king out of his swine later coax a dying god out of a tree, one verse at a time, and the same wand that punishes him he is finally trusted to hold. The Fourth Branch's calm is that magic and justice are one craft: to know the true shape of a thing — a name, a name-day, a wound, a woman made of flowers — is to be able to change it, and to be answerable for the change. Gwydion is the enchanter who learns, and teaches, that power over forms is a form of responsibility. Original script note: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Gwydion (the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest), and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. The plain-ASCII domain gwydion.com is registered to a third party and held outside the collection; it is watched for release. Until then this temple stands without a domain of its own.

title: Love, Youth, Poetry
text: Love, Youth, Poetry: The Mac Óc — the Son of the Young, god of Brú na Bóinne Aengus — Old Irish Óengus, the mac ind Óc, 'son of the young' — is the ever-young god of the Túatha Dé Danann, son of [[dagda|the Dagda]] and Bóand, the goddess of the Boyne. His dossier is the strangest kind of power in the Irish corpus: not the club or the spear, but the dream, the bargain, and the unaging house. He was conceived and born in a single day the sun was made to hold still; he won the greatest mound in Ireland on a quibble of grammar; he loved a girl he had seen only in sleep, and found her by searching every lake in Ireland for a year. Where his father's strength is provision, his is patience: the young god who waits out time itself. The Dream: In the Aislinge Óenguso a maiden comes to him in sleep with music; he sickens for love of a woman he has never seen awake, and the dream must be hunted like a quarry. The Swan: Caer Ibormeith lives one year as a girl and one as a swan among a hundred and fifty swans on Loch Bél Dracon; to win her, Óengus takes the swan-shape himself. Brú na Bóinne: The Brug on the Boyne — síd in Broga, the mound the world calls Newgrange — his Otherworld house, won from the Dagda for 'a day and a night' and kept ever since. The Day and the Night: Asked when he would surrender the mound lent 'for a day and a night', he answered that the whole world is spent in days and nights — and the answer has never been overturned. Symbols: Brú na Bóinne — The Brug on the Boyne, his unaging house — the síd the tales call síd in Broga and the world calls Newgrange; The swan-shape — The form he takes at Samain on Loch Bél Dracon to win Caer Ibormeith — love answered in kind, shape for shape; The dream (aisling) — The maiden's nightly visit with her timpán — desire that arrives before its object, and must be pursued into the waking world; The day and the night — The quibble that holds the Brug forever — time itself parsed as a loan without a term; The crystal bower — The grianán he built at the Brug for Étaín in her fly-shape — shelter given to a hunted woman when no one else could hold her Aengus's mythology is a study in winning without fighting. The three great set-pieces — his birth inside a stopped day, his taking of the Brug, and the dream-quest for Caer Ibormeith — are all victories of time: time held still, time parsed, time waited out. Cath Maige Tuired and Tochmarc Étaíne add the counselor and the host: the son whose wit saves his father, and the keeper of the Brug who shelters Étaín when the whole of Ireland has no safer room. Tochmarc Étaíne: The Day the Sun Stood Still The Dagda desired Bóand, the wife of Elcmar of the Brug, and sent Elcmar away on a day's errand to Bres. To hide what followed, the tale says, the Dagda made the sun stand still: nine months passed, and the world reckoned it a single day — so the child was conceived and born within one day, and Elcmar came home none the wiser. They named the boy Óengus, but the story gave him the name that stuck: mac ind Óc, 'the son of the young', because young was the day that bore him. The episode fixes the god's signature before he can speak: he is a child of bent time. Bóand, the Boyne itself made goddess, is his mother; the Dagda, the All-Father, his sire; and his first house is the river-bend his father stole a day to give him. The fosterage that followed — with Midir of Brí Léith — placed him among the proudest of the Túatha Dé Danann and set up every tale that came after. De Gabáil in t-Sída: A Day and a Night When the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the Túatha Dé Danann, Óengus was away fostered with Midir and received nothing. He came home to claim his share, and the Dagda, having no mound left to give, granted him Brú na Bóinne — the Dagda's own house — for a day and a night. When the term was spent and the Dagda asked for his Brug back, Óengus answered that it is in days and nights that the whole world is spent, and so the grant had no end. The All-Father lost the argument, and the greatest mound in Ireland passed to the son who had read the fine print. The tale is told with a straight face, but its logic is the logic of the síd itself: the Otherworld does not run on mortal clocks. A god born inside a single stretched day is the natural owner of a house held on a day without a term. Irish law prized the exact word; Óengus's first deed makes etymology into real estate. Aislinge Óenguso: The Dream of Óengus A maiden came to Óengus in sleep, playing a timpán, the sweetest music he had heard; for a year she came, and for a year he could not touch her, and when she ceased to come he wasted with love-sickness. The physicians of the Túatha Dé Danann could not cure him, for his sickness was a woman who existed somewhere in the world. Bóand his mother searched Ireland for a year and found nothing; the Dagda searched a year and found nothing; then Bodb Derg, king of the síd of Munster, searched, and at the year's end found her: Caer Ibormeith, daughter of Ethal Anbuail of síd Uaman in Connacht. But Caer lived under a rhythm no bargain could break: she spent one year in girl's shape and one as a swan, among nine score swans on Loch Bél Dracon, and the change came at Samain. Óengus went to the lake at Samain and saw them, each pair of swans linked by a silver chain, Caer's own chain of gold about her neck. He called to her, and she answered that she would go with him only if he took the swan-shape beside her. He entered the water, became a swan, and they flew three times around the lake — and their music put every listener to sleep for three days and three nights — then away to Brú na Bóinne, where the singing of the two swans became part of the mound's music ever after. Tochmarc Étaíne: The Bower of the Purple Fly When the jealous Fuamnach struck Étaín with a rod of scarlet quicken-tree and made her a pool of water, then a worm, then a purple fly, the fly that was Étaín came at last to Brú na Bóinne, to the hall of Óengus. He knew her — the fly's music and its radiance were hers — and he built her a grianán, a sun-bower of crystal filled with healing herbs and the bloom of every field, and she stayed with him there, and the window of the bower let her pass in and out as she pleased. It could not last. Fuamnach followed the rumor of the fly's good fortune and raised a magic wind that swept Étaín out of the bower and across Ireland for seven years, until she fell into the cup of Étar's wife at the Bay of Cíú and was drunk, conceived, and born again a thousand and twelve years after her first birth. Óengus's shelter is one of the gentlest episodes in the cycle: the young god keeping one hunted woman safe in the safest house in Ireland, against a malice even his Brug could not finally exclude. Cath Maige Tuired: The Satirist's Three Gold Coins Under the tyranny of Bres the Dagda was set to building the usurper's forts, and the satirist Cridenbél taxed him the three best bits of every ration, until the greatest of the gods was failing from hunger — for no one dared refuse a satirist whose curse raised blisters on the face. Óengus came to his father and gave him the counsel that turned the trap: demand of Bres the pick of the cattle of Ireland as wages, and hide three gold coins in the porridge portion meant for the satirist. Cridenbél swallowed greed and gold together and died of it; and when Bres demanded the Dagda's death for the killing, the dead man's own belly gave the verdict — cut open, it held the gold, proof that greed and not the Dagda had killed him. The episode is the tradition's clearest pairing of father and son: the Dagda's patience carrying the labor, Óengus's wit carrying the case. The young god does not raise a weapon in the whole of Cath Maige Tuired, and does not need to — his contribution to the war that freed the Túatha Dé Danann was a sentence spoken at the right fireside. Syncretism: The comparison the handbooks prefer for Óengus runs to Gaul and Wales rather than to Rome. The Gaulish Maponos , 'the Divine Son' — known from dedications to Apollo Maponus in the Roman north of Britain and from the Ravenna Cosmography's locus Maponi — is the same figure-type: the ever-young son of a greater divine parent. Mac Cana and Sjoestedt set Maponos beside both Óengus and the Welsh Mabon ap Modron , 'Son son of Mother', the hunter-youth of Culhwch ac Olwen whose name is built on the same Proto-Celtic words *makwos, 'son', and *mātīr, 'mother'. The popular handbooks go further and call Óengus 'the Irish Eros'; the medieval texts give a stranger and more specific figure — a god of dream, youth, and cunning whose love-story is won by patience and shape-changing rather than by arrows. The comparisons are structural and instructive; no inscription identifies him, and the identification of Maponos with Mabon is itself a scholarly argument, not a fact. Cultural legacy: No Irish god had a better literary afterlife than the young one. W. B. Yeats made him a byword for longing itself in 'The Song of Wandering Aengus' (1899) — the hazel wand, the fire in the head, the glimmering girl with apple blossom in her hair who called his name and ran — a poem that poured the Aislinge into the bloodstream of modern English verse. James Stephens gave him speaking parts and moods in The Crock of Gold (1912), where Angus Og wanders the Irish countryside being wise and young. In the later Gaelic tradition he never faded: the Fenian tale of Diarmaid and Gráinne keeps him at Brú na Bóinne as Diarmaid's fosterer and protector, and Irish folklore kept the Brug as his house into the modern period. His name took a second, quieter path: worn to Angus, it became one of the most familiar masculine names in Scotland — a theonym hiding in plain sight on every map of Angus and in every roll of Scottish kings. And his address became the most visited prehistoric site in Ireland: Newgrange, where five thousand winters of sun have entered the chamber the tales assigned to the son of the young. Extended meditation: Aengus is the god of the interval — the stretch of time between wanting and having, and his whole dossier asks what can be done with it. His father held the sun still for nine months to make a day large enough to be born in; the son learned the lesson and spent his career proving that time is a text to be parsed, not a wall to be stormed. A loan of a day and a night is forever, if you read it right. A dream that comes nightly for a year is an address, if you are willing to search every lake in Ireland for it. The name says the same: óen-gus, one vigor, a single strength held undivided — no club, no cauldron, no host, just the one force applied without distraction. That is why his love-story is the corpus's gentlest. Every other divine wooing in Irish myth is a raid, a riddle, or a revenge; Óengus's is a search. He does not seize Caer Ibormeith; he finds her, asks her, accepts her condition, and meets her in her own shape — a god who becomes a swan because the girl is one. The music the two swans make, which puts the world to sleep for three days, is the dream coming back around: the aisling that began as a haunting ends as a harmony. Youth, in this mythology, is not the season of appetite. It is the season before resignation — the one vigor that has not yet learned to stop looking. Original script note: The normalized Old Irish form is Óengus , written in the Insular Latin script of the medieval manuscripts, with a síneadh fada marking the long Ó; the Middle Irish spelling Aengus drops the accent, and the temple follows that unaccented form. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the restored form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: aengus.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Otherworld, Underworld
text: Otherworld, Underworld: The Deep, the Abyss — realm of the feast and the hunt Annwn is the Welsh Otherworld of the Mabinogi and the oldest Welsh poetry — a realm of plenty where the feast never fails, ruled in the First Branch by [[arawn|Arawn]], and hunted across by Gwyn ap Nudd, whom God set over the demons of Annwn lest they destroy this world. Its cauldron, borne home from its fortresses at terrible cost, is the oldest quest of Arthurian tradition. The Cauldron of the Head of Annwn: Kindled by the breath of nine maidens, rimmed with pearls, it will not boil a coward's food — the prize of Arthur's voyage in Preiddeu Annwfn. The Hounds of Annwn: Arawn's pack — gleaming white with red ears, the colours the Welsh tradition gives every creature from the Otherworld. Prydwen: Arthur's ship on the voyage to the fortresses of Annwn — three full loads went in; except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi. The Hunt of Gwyn ap Nudd: The son of Nudd rides with the hunt of Annwn; in Culhwch ac Olwen, God set him over its demons lest they destroy this world. Symbols: The cauldron of Pen Annwn — Plenty that will not serve the coward — abundance that answers only to courage; White hounds with red ears — The colours of the Otherworld made flesh — beauty that marks the boundary crossed; Caer Sidi and the fortresses — The revolving castle and its sister fortresses — the Otherworld as architecture that must be won, not visited; Prydwen — Arthur's ship — the voyage into the deep from which only seven returned; The year's exchange — Arawn and Pwyll trading shapes and kingdoms — the Otherworld close enough to wear a man's face Annwn is named in the very first pages of the Mabinogi and in the most difficult poem of early Welsh tradition. Its dossier is small and immense: a king who trades his shape, a cauldron that will not boil a coward's food, a hunt that keeps the world's demons leashed — and, behind all three, the deep itself. Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed (First Branch): The Year in Annwn Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, is hunting in Glyn Cuch when he drives a strange pack off a stag — hounds gleaming white, with red ears, the colours of the Otherworld — and feeds his own dogs on the kill. Their master rides up: [[arawn|Arawn]], a king of Annwn, and the offense is real. To make amends Pwyll accepts Arawn's bargain: for a year and a day they will exchange shapes and kingdoms, and at the year's end Pwyll must face Arawn's rival Hafgan — a king who can be killed by a single blow only; strike him twice and by the next day he fights as strongly as before. Pwyll rules Annwn for the year in Arawn's likeness, in a court of unsurpassed plenty — and each night lies beside Arawn's queen without once touching her. At the appointed ford he strikes Hafgan once, refuses the second blow the wounded king begs for, and Annwn is united under Arawn. When the two kings meet again at Glyn Cuch and resume their own shapes, Arawn learns of the year's chastity and the friendship is sealed with gifts of horses, greyhounds, hawks, and gold. From that day Pwyll was called not Pwyll Prince of Dyfed but Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll, Head of Annwn. Preiddeu Annwfn (Book of Taliesin): The Spoils of Annwn The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwfn', preserved in the fourteenth-century Book of Taliesin and spoken in the poet's own voice, is the oldest surviving account of an Arthurian Otherworld raid. Arthur sails in his ship Prydwen against the fortresses of the deep — Caer Sidi, Caer Pedryfan, Caer Wydyr, and the rest — and the refrain tolls after each: 'except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.' Three full loads of Prydwen went into Annwn; seven men came back. The prize is the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — kindled by the breath of nine maidens, its rim set about with pearls, and marked by the rule the Welsh tradition fixes on Otherworld vessels: it will not boil the food of a coward. The poem is elliptical, proud, and mournful at once — the poet stands apart from the swordsmen who went in and never came out — but its facts became permanent: the Otherworld has a cauldron, Arthur went to get it, and almost no one returned. Culhwch ac Olwen: Gwyn ap Nudd and the Demons of Annwn The great hunting catalogue of Culhwch ac Olwen names its most uncanny huntsman: Gwyn ap Nudd, son of Nudd — 'God has set him over the demons of Annwn, lest this world be destroyed.' The hunt of the boar Twrch Trwyth cannot be accomplished without him, and so Gwyn rides out of Annwn at Arthur's muster: the Otherworld's own power, conscripted to keep its worst inhabitants leashed. The same tale gives Gwyn his famous quarrel. He had carried off Creiddylad, daughter of Lludd, from her father's house, and Gwythyr ap Greidawl raised a host and took her back; Arthur judged between them — the maiden to remain with her father, and the two to fight for her every May Day until the Day of Judgment, when the winner takes her for good. Gwyn's hunt is therefore not seasonal sport but a standing order: Annwn's violence rides out under a king who is himself a covenant. Buchedd Collen: The King on Glastonbury Tor The Welsh Life of St Collen gives Annwn its most local address. Collen, keeping his hermitage under Glastonbury Tor, hears two men say that Gwyn ap Nudd — king of Annwn and of the Tylwyth Teg, the Fair Folk — holds his court above. Collen answers that the hosts of the air are demons; a summons follows, and on the summit he finds a castle of the utmost splendour, the king on a golden chair, and a banquet of dishes he has never seen the like of. Collen sprinkles his holy water over the food, and the whole vision dissolves — castle, court, and king gone as if they had never been, leaving the saint standing on the green Tor. The tale is late and Christian, but it keeps the old facts in place: Gwyn is king of Annwn, his hall is a feast beyond earthly measure, and the Otherworld can open on a hillside in Somerset and close again without a trace. Syncretism: Annwn's clearest kin are Irish: the síd of the Túatha Dé Danann, where the feast likewise never fails — the Dagda's cauldron of Murias, from which no company went away unsatisfied, is the standing comparison for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and Mac Cana sets the two vessels side by side as one Celtic figure-type. The Irish Otherworld of the immrama and echtrai — Mag Mell, Emain Ablach, lands 'without grief, without sorrow, without death' — matches Annwn's profile point for point: plenty, beauty, and the suspension of age and sickness. Yet the Brythonic tradition is not a copy of the Gaelic one: no Irish text knows the name Annwn, and the Welsh corpus built its Otherworld on its own geography — the ford at Glyn Cuch, the revolving fortresses of the Taliesin poem, the Tor at Glastonbury. The Christian redactors left the structure intact while re-labelling its inhabitants: by Buchedd Collen, Gwyn ap Nudd's splendid court could be dismissed as a demonic glamour without surrendering one detail of the feast. Cultural legacy: Preiddeu Annwfn stands at the head of the Arthurian tradition: the raid on the Otherworld fortresses is older than every romance of the Grail, and scholars from Loomis onward have read the quest for the Head of Annwn's cauldron — a vessel of plenty that tests the worthy — as the Grail story's deepest Welsh root. The name kept working in Welsh: Annwn remains the living word for the Otherworld, and the white red-eared hounds became the Cŵn Annwn of later Welsh folklore, the pack whose crying in the night sky foretells a death. Gwyn ap Nudd rode out of the texts into modern Druidry and pagan practice as the great huntsman and psychopomp of the Welsh tradition, and Glastonbury Tor — crowned now by the stump of St Michael's tower — still carries his court in the popular imagination. Restoring Annwn in Unicode costs nothing and fixes something: the canonical spelling of the deep, held against the drift of anglicized spellings like Annwvyn and Annwyn. Extended meditation: Annwn is the rare Otherworld whose name tells you where it is: an- + dwfn, the un-deep, the very deep — not a land over the sea or under a hill but the depth beneath the world, the place the surface world is the skin of. The tradition never pretends it is far away. Pwyll stumbles into it on an ordinary hunt by breaking an ordinary courtesy; it lies a year's shape-shift away, close enough for two kings to trade faces and governments across it. And its gifts all carry a price exacted in courage. The feast is boundless, but the cauldron will not boil a coward's food; the voyage is possible, but except seven none returned; the hunt rides out, but it rides to keep the demons of the deep leashed for the world's sake. Annwn is the Celtic imagination's answer to the question of what lies underneath: plenty without limit, behind a door that only opens once — and a word for it, five plain letters, that still means the deep. Original script note: Welsh has been written in the Latin alphabet throughout its manuscript history, and the normalized form Annwn is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. The manuscripts spell the name Annwfn (Middle Welsh f writes the voiced [v]); the modern normalized spelling is Annwn. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: annwn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The King of Annwn
text: The King of Annwn: Otherworld, Annwn Arawn is the king of Annwn, the Welsh Otherworld: the lord whose white, red-eared hounds bring down a stag in Pwyll's hunting-ground at Glyn Cuch, and whose answer to the insult is the strangest exchange in the Mabinogi — a year and a day in which two kings trade faces, thrones, and beds, so that honor may be tested where no one is watching. The White Hounds: Arawn's pack, shining white with red ears — the colour of the Otherworld, a sight Pwyll had never seen on any hound of his own. The Exchange of Shapes: A year and a day in which Arawn takes Pwyll's form in Dyfed and Pwyll takes Arawn's in Annwn — and neither court suspects. The Ford: The appointed meeting-place where Pwyll must face Hafgan, king of the other realm of Annwn — with one blow and no more. The Untouched Bed: Arawn's queen, the fairest woman Pwyll had ever seen — with whom he shares a bed for a year and never turns his face to her. Symbols: The white hounds with red ears — The colour of the Otherworld — a hunt that arrives from the far side of the boundary; The exchanged shape — Kingship as a trust held for another: the year Arawn's face ruled two realms; The single blow — Restraint as the condition of victory — strike once, or not at all; The untouched bed — Honor kept in the dark, where no one would ever have known; The ford — The meeting-place between realms, where debts are paid and blows are counted; The yearly gifts — Friendship renewed in kind — horses, greyhounds, hawks, and treasure Arawn's whole dossier is one story, and it is the opening movement of the Mabinogi: the hunting-debt at Glyn Cuch and the year-long exchange that turns an insult into the strongest friendship in Welsh prose. Every word of it is preserved in the First Branch, Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed. First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed: The Wrong at Glyn Cuch Pwyll, lord of Dyfed, goes hunting at Glyn Cuch, and there he sees a sight he has never seen: a pack of hounds shining white with red ears bringing down a stag. He drives them off and sets his own hounds on the kill — and the stranger who rides up is Arawn, king of Annwn, and it was his hunt. Arawn names the discourtesy plainly: he will not take revenge, but a man who feeds his hounds on another's kill has wronged him, and Pwyll offers to buy back his friendship at whatever price. Arawn names it. He has a rival, Hafgan, king of the other realm of Annwn, who wars on him without end; let Pwyll take Arawn's shape and his place for a year and a day, and meet Hafgan at the ford at the year's turning. First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed: The Exchange of Shapes Each king takes the other's form and goes to the other's court, and neither realm suspects. Arawn rules Dyfed so well that there had never been so good a year in it. Pwyll enters Annwn in Arawn's likeness, and that first night he is led to the bed of Arawn's wife — the fairest and most comely woman he had ever seen. He turns his back to her, and he does so every night of the year: he speaks to her with courtesy by day, and in the bed he never once turns his face toward her. The queen never knows. The whole test of the tale is here, in the dark, where no one could have seen the difference. First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed: The Single Blow at the Ford Arawn's instructions were exact: Hafgan — the name suggests 'Summer-White' — can be slain by one blow, and only one; strike him a second time and he will rise as strong as before and fight again the next day. At the appointed time the two kings meet at the ford, and at the first clash Pwyll strikes Hafgan one blow that shears through his shield and armour, and Hafgan knows he is dead. 'For God's sake,' he begs, 'finish me' — and Pwyll refuses: the stroke he gave is all Hafgan will have from him. Hafgan's nobles declare their king lost, and Pwyll takes the submission and hostages of Hafgan's realm, so that the two kingdoms of Annwn are made one under Arawn's crown. First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed: The Restoration and the Title The two kings meet again at the ford where they had arranged it, each in his own shape, and embrace and go home. Arawn's queen, rejoicing at his return, remarks that he has not spoken to her as he does tonight for a whole year — and Arawn praises God for a friend so true. In Dyfed, Pwyll's court hears the story and tells him he did well to make such a friend. From that time the two realms send each other gifts every year: horses and greyhounds and hawks, and every kind of treasure they think will please. And because Pwyll had ruled Annwn and joined its two kingdoms in one, he was called from then on Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll Head of Annwn — in place of Pwyll lord of Dyfed. Later Welsh tradition: The Hounds and the Spoils of Annwn The Mabinogi never brings Arawn back on stage, but his world keeps growing. The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwn', preserved in the Book of Taliesin, sends Arthur's men to raid the Otherworld for the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — Pen Annwfn, the very title the First Branch gives Pwyll's honour — and only seven come home. The poem never names Annwn's king, and honest scholarship leaves it unnamed. Later Welsh folklore knows the Cŵn Annwn, the Hounds of Annwn — white with red ears, exactly Arawn's pack — whose baying across the night sky was heard as a death-omen, and folk tradition gave their mastery to Gwyn ap Nudd rather than to Arawn. The hounds outgrew their first master; the year of the exchange did not. Syncretism: Arawn's comparisons are almost all inward, and the Welsh corpus itself supplies them. His clearest rival for the kingship of the Otherworld is Gwyn ap Nudd, whom Culhwch ac Olwen says God set over the demons of Annwn — a second king of Annwn in a second text, and the folklore gave Gwyn the hounds that the Mabinogi gave Arawn. The structural reading runs deeper: commentators since Mac Cana have read the Annwn adventure as the proving of Pwyll's character before the coming of [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] — the hero tested in honor and restraint in the Otherworld before the Otherworld's queen chooses him in this one. The name itself may be the tale's one foreign guest: Ifor Williams proposed that Arawn is a learned borrowing of the biblical Aaron, carried into Welsh by Latin learning, and the handbooks register the possibility without deciding it. No Gaulish or Irish counterpart of Arawn has ever been convincingly proposed; the exchange-of-kings motif is the Mabinogi's own. Cultural legacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Arawn out of the White and Red Books and into English, and the white red-eared hounds entered the stock of Celtic imagery from that day. In the twentieth century the figure found his widest audience inverted: Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain (1964–68) made 'Arawn Death-Lord of Annuvin' the arch-villain of five children's novels, and Disney's The Black Cauldron (1985) kept the dark-lord version on screen — a long way from the most honorable king in Welsh prose, but the reason the name is known worldwide. The Cŵn Annwn meanwhile never left Welsh folklore, still baying as a death-omen in folk memory into the modern period. Modern Druid and pagan practice honours Arawn as lord of the Otherworld and patron of kept faith, and the name survives in Wales as a rare living given name. Extended meditation: Arawn sets the one test that cannot be cheated: he gives a stranger his face, his throne, and his bed, and waits a year to learn what the stranger is. Everything Pwyll does in Annwn is invisible — no one in either kingdom can tell the kings apart, and no one will ever know what passed in the bed unless the doer confesses it. That is exactly the point. Honor, the First Branch argues, is what a man does when the only witness is himself. The tale rewards it without sentimentality: the kept faith becomes an unbroken friendship, an otherworld alliance, the title Pen Annwfn, and a court that tells its lord he chose his friend well. Arawn's kingdom is the far side of the world, but his question is asked everywhere: who are you when no one is watching? Original script note: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Arawn — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: arawn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/arawn/ in the meantime.

title: Battle, Death, Crow
text: Battle, Death, Crow: The Scald-Crow of the Battlefield Badb is the Irish war-goddess whose name is her shape: badb , the scald-crow — the grey-and-black hooded crow that walks the battlefield when the spears have done their work. She is one of the three of war whom the Lebor Gabála calls the daughters of Ernmas — Badb, Macha, and Anand, the Morrígan — and the Táin gives her its most terrible sound: the shriek over the marching hosts that kills men with fear before a blow is struck. She never fights; she foretells, she panics, and she gathers what the battle leaves. Badb Catha: 'Crow of battle' — her standing title in the texts: the bird that haunts the field and the goddess who owns it are one word. The Shriek over the Hosts: At Gáirech and Irgáirech, the Táin says, Badb and Bé Néit and Némain shrieked above the armies until a hundred warriors fell dead of fright. The Ford: The boundary water where the war-goddess stands washing — the Morrígan at the ford of the Unius, the washer of the doomed in the later Gaelic tradition. The Daughters of Ernmas: Badb, Macha, and Anand — the triple face of Irish war, three sisters of one mother whom the sources also call by the single name Morrígan. Symbols: The scald-crow — The hooded crow, grey and black — her name, her shape, and her retinue on every field; The shriek — Panic as a weapon: the sound that kills men with fear before the spear is thrown; The ford — The boundary between bank and bank, living and dead — the water where the doomed are read; The triad — Badb, Macha, Némain: the three of war, one terror in three voices; The washing of spoils — The harness and garments of the soon-dead, rinsed in the ford before the battle that will bloody them Badb's dossier is genealogy, sound, and omen rather than adventure: she is the sister in the list, the voice over the army, the bird on the pillar-stone. The Lebor Gabála fixes her family, the Táin fixes her weapon, and the death-tales fix her posture — and the commentators have spent a century and a half working out where she ends and her sisters begin. Lebor Gabála Érenn: The Daughters of Ernmas The Lebor Gabála Érenn, Ireland's medieval book of invasions, gives the war-goddesses their pedigree: 'Badb and Macha and Anand, of whom are the Paps of Anu in Luachair, were the three daughters of Ernmas the she-farmer.' The verse recension sings the same family in another key — 'Badb and Macha, greatness of wealth, Morrígu, springs of craftiness, sources of bitter fighting, were the three daughters of Ernmas' — so that the tradition itself is of two minds: sometimes the Morrígan is the third sister, sometimes the single name for all three. The same book marries her into the house of the war-god. Neit son of Indui, the god of battle, had two wives — Badb and Nemain — and the pedigree records the slaying of the three of them at Ailech by the Fomorians. Cormac's Glossary had already fixed the marriage in the language of record: Neith, the god of battle among the pagan Gael, and Nemon his wife. Badb is never an isolated figure; she is a sister and a wife in a family whose whole business is war. Táin Bó Cúailnge: The Shriek over the Hosts When the men of Ireland march under [[medb|Medb]] for the brown bull of Cooley, the Táin marks the nights of the hosting with the sound of the war-goddesses: 'Badb and Bé Néit and Némain shrieked above them that night in Gáirech and Irgáirech, so that a hundred of their warriors fell dead of fright.' It is the battle's true opening — the killing has begun before a single spear is cast, and its instrument is a voice. The passage tells you everything about her method. She does not wound; she announces. The shriek over the column is prophecy delivered as noise, the knowledge of the field's end injected into the march at its beginning — and the Irish phrase for the whole business of battlefield terror, badb catha , the crow of battle, is simply her name at work as a common noun. Cath Maige Tuired: The War-Goddess at Mag Tuired The Second Battle of Mag Tuired, the war the Túatha Dé Danann fight against the Fomorians, runs on the war-goddess's work from its eve to its aftermath. On Samain night [[dagda|the Dagda]] met the Morrígan at the ford of the Unius in Connacht, where she stood washing with one foot on either bank; they lay together at the ford, and she pledged herself to the Túatha Dé Danann's cause, promising to bring the hearts of the Fomorian host and the blood of their king Indech. After [[lugh|Lugh]]'s sling-stone felled [[balor|Balor]] and the Fomorians broke, it was the Morrígan who proclaimed the battle and the rout to the royal heights of Ireland and its síd-hosts, and who uttered the great prophecy — 'Peace up to heaven, heaven down to earth, earth beneath heaven' — and then its darker twin, the vision of the world's ending. The commentators note that the texts keep the sisters' voices interchangeable: what the manuscript gives to the Morrígan, the tradition hears also in Badb's register, and the Lebor Gabála had already made them one family. Aided Con Culainn: The Crow on the Pillar-Stone Cú Chulainn's death-tale, Brislech Mór Maige Muirthemni, gives the crow-goddesses the last word over the greatest of the Ulster heroes. Mortally wounded at Muirthemne, [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]] lashed himself to a pillar-stone so that he would die on his feet, and for three days his enemies would not close in, uncertain whether he lived. Then the battle-goddess Morrígu came with her sisters in the form of scald-crows and settled on his shoulder — and Erc said, 'That pillar is not wont to be under birds,' and only then did the host dare approach and take the hero's head. It is the emblematic scene of her whole dossier: the scald-crow is the signature of death itself, the field's first and final reader. The living man keeps her off; the dead man is her perch. Gaelic Tradition: The Washer at the Ford The medieval texts give the war-goddess her washing-place — the Morrígan washing at the ford of the Unius on the eve of Mag Tuired — and the later Gaelic tradition gives the figure her full shape: the washer at the ford, the woman seen at the boundary water rinsing the blood-stained garments and harness of those about to die in battle. In Scottish Gaelic folklore she is the bean nighe, the washerwoman whose sight foretells death, and the commentators, Mac Cana among them, treat her as the folk continuation of the Badb's own figure. The washing is prophecy, not threat. The doom is already written — the garments in her hands belong to men still alive and armed — and she merely launders the evidence. No Irish figure holds the moment before death so patiently: not the blow, not the battle, but the foreknowledge, rinsed clean in running water. Syncretism: Badb's clearest cross-border witness is Gaulish, and it is exact. An altar from Mieussy in Haute-Savoie dedicates to Cathubodua — *catu-*bodwā, 'battle-crow' — the precise reverse compound of Irish badb catha . Delamarre and Koch treat the two names as one formation across the Celtic languages: the crow of battle named in stone on the continent and in saga in Ireland. The Welsh corpus, by contrast, is silent on her — no figure of the Mabinogi continues the name, and the Brythonic silence is recorded rather than repaired. Typological comparison has set her beside the Norse valkyries, the raven-feeding choosers of the slain; the handbooks note the parallel without claiming descent. Within the lexicon her closest kin are her own sisters, [[morrigan|the Mórrígan]] and [[macha|Macha]], and the war she prophesied binds her to [[dagda|the Dagda]], [[lugh|Lugh]], and [[nuada|Nuadu]]. Cultural legacy: The crow of battle rode the Celtic revival in English dress. W. M. Hennessy's 'The Ancient Irish Goddess of War' (Revue Celtique, 1870) had already gathered the Morrígan material for scholars, and Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried Cath Maige Tuired and its war-goddesses to a wide reading public, crow-form and prophecy complete. Modern fantasy and games have made the war-goddess's crow-shape one of the stock images of the genre, and contemporary pagan practice honors Badb among the three of the Morrígan. In the Irish language the word never needed reviving: badhbh has meant the hooded crow all along, and the grey bird on the battlefield needed no gloss for any Irish hearer. Across the water, the Scottish bean nighe kept her folk shape washing at the ford deep into the era of the great folklore collections. Extended meditation: Badb is the rare theonym that refuses to be a metaphor: the word for the bird and the name of the goddess are one, and the medieval writers never felt the need to choose between them. To name her is already to say what she does. Other gods have attributes; she has a species — the grey scald-crow that comes down to the field when the field is finished, and the texts simply ask us to understand that the bird knew all along. Her power is the moment before. In no surviving text does she strike a blow: she shrieks over the marching column, washes at the boundary water, settles on the pillar-stone — the goddess of foreknowledge and of aftermath, of everything in a battle except the fighting. That is not a small dossier but a strange and exact one: she is what war feels like to those who already know its end. The name keeps the question open in every grey bird on a fence-post: if you could see the end of the day at its beginning, what would you do with the hours between? Original script note: The normalized Old Irish form is Badb — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: badb.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The King of the Evil Eye
text: The King of the Evil Eye: The Venomed Gaze, the Fomorian Tribute, the Fortress of Tory, the Grandson's Stone Balor — Balor Béimnech, 'Balor of the Mighty Blows' — is king of the Fomorians, the sea-borne oppressors of medieval Irish tradition, and owner of the most feared weapon in the whole corpus: a single eye so venomed by the fumes of a druids' brew that no army could stand before its gaze. Grandfather of Lugh and doomed by that very grandson's sling-stone at Mag Tuired, he is the Irish tradition's great figure of destructive sovereignty — power that poisons its possessor and is answered, in the end, by his own blood. The Venomed Eye: One eye, poisoned in boyhood by the fumes of a druids' charm-brew; any army it looked upon was worthless, though it were many thousands strong. The Fomorian Tribute: Under Balor and Indech the Fomorians taxed Ireland from the sea, and set the very gods to serf-work until Mag Tuired broke the yoke. The Tower of Tory: In the Donegal oral tradition, the sea-girt tower where Balor prisoned his daughter Eithne against the prophecy of a grandson's hand. The Grandson's Stone: Lugh's sling-stone at Mag Tuired drove the eye backward through Balor's head, so that its own gaze blasted the Fomorian host. Symbols: The venomed eye — A weapon the owner cannot aim without an army to raise the lid — power that outgrew its possessor; The polished lid-lifter — Four men with a handle passed through the eyelid — kingship reduced to machinery, a gaze other men must operate; The tower of Tory — The sea-girt prison built against a prophecy — the fortress that made the doom it feared; The Glas Gaibhnenn — The grey-green cow Balor stole from Cian in the oral tradition — the theft that set the grandson's birth in motion; The sling-stone — The small, aimed answer to the vast, unaimed gaze — the grandson's hand the druids foretold Balor's dossier is short and total: he exists in the tradition to be the thing that must be brought down. Cath Maige Tuired gives him the war's most famous single stroke, the Lebor Gabála fixes his lineage and his wife's revenge, and the Donegal oral tradition supplies the prophecy, the tower, and the stolen cow that medieval manuscripts only glance at. Lebor Gabála Érenn: Balor Son of Dot, Grandson of Nét The book of invasions fixes Balor's place before it tells his deeds: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, 'Balor son of Dot, grandson of Nét', king of the Fomorians — the sea-going race who had pressed on Ireland since the age of the Nemedians, exacting tribute from the outer islands. His wife was Cethlenn of the crooked teeth, and it was her spear, or the wound she dealt at Mag Tuired, that killed the Dagda at the Brug years later — the Lebor Gabála records the All-Father's death from Cethlenn's blow as the long-settled price of Balor's war. His daughter was Ethniu, and she was given to Cian, son of Dian Cécht the healer; their son was Lugh, the Samildánach, equally skilled in all arts. Thus the Fomorian king was the grandfather of the Túatha Dé Danann's deliverer — the genealogy that the whole tragedy of Mag Tuired turns on. Cath Maige Tuired: How the Eye Was Poisoned Cath Maige Tuired explains the weapon before it uses it. Balor had a destructive eye, never opened except on a battlefield, and four men were needed to raise its lid with a polished handle that passed through it. Any army that eye looked upon was made worthless, though it were many thousands strong. The poison had a childhood. When Balor was a boy, his father's druids were brewing a charm, and the boy looked in on the work; the fumes of the brew rose and struck the eye, and from that day its gaze was venom. The detail is the tradition's whole theory of the figure in one image: power taken in unguarded, as a child takes in smoke, and carried incurably for a lifetime. The Oral Tradition (Tory Island): The Tower and the Prophecy The medieval manuscripts know that Ethniu was Balor's daughter and Lugh's mother; how that came to be is told by the oral tradition of the north-west, collected in the nineteenth century on and around Tory Island — Balor's sea-girt fortress off the Donegal coast. A druid foretold that Balor would die by the hand of his own grandson, and the king answered the prophecy with masonry: he locked his daughter Eithne in a tower on the rock, with twelve matrons to keep every man from her sight. The doom came in by the usual door. Balor coveted the Glas Gaibhnenn, the grey-green cow of Cian, and stole her across the water; Cian crossed to Tory for redress, and with the help of the druidess Biróg won into the tower in woman's dress and to Eithne's side. When the child was born Balor had him cast into the sea — but the sea gave him back, fostered and hidden, until a young stranger called Lugh came to Nuadu's court at Tara and was asked what art he practiced. The question the Fomorians could not answer had been growing up under their own doom all along. Cath Maige Tuired: The Sling-Stone at Mag Tuired At the second battle of Mag Tuired the armies broke each other all day, and then Balor came against the Túatha Dé Danann with the Fomorian host, destroying and slaughtering. He commanded that the lid of his eye be raised, so that he might blast the enemy with its look — and the four men set the polished handle to the lid. It was then that Lugh cast a sling-stone at him, which carried the eye backward through his head, so that it was his own host that looked into it. Balor fell on top of the Fomorian fighting-men, and twenty-seven of them died beneath his side. The weapon the Fomorians had built their tyranny on spent its last gaze on its owners — and the battle turned with the eye. Afterward the Túatha Dé Danann took the tribute back from the defeated host, and the power of the Fomorians over Ireland was broken for good. Syncretism: Balor's clearest cross-border witnesses are comparative, not cognate. The Welsh corpus preserves no figure derived from the same name — the Brythonic silence is total, as it is for so many of the Fomorian cycle. The parallels the scholarship actually leans on are typological. First, the Greek Acrisius : the king who prisoned his daughter Danae in a bronze chamber because a prophecy named her son his slayer, and died by that grandson Perseus all the same — the Eithne tower is the same tale-shape, and comparatists have set the two side by side since the nineteenth century. Second, the one-eyed monster answered by aimed cunning — the Polyphemus pattern — where the single enormous eye is both the ogre's strength and the one place he can be struck. Third, and nearest home, the Irish and Mediterranean complex of the evil eye itself: the belief that a look can wither cattle, milk, and men, which Sjoestedt and Mac Cana both treat as the living folk-ground of Balor's venomed gaze. O'Rahilly read him further, as a figure of death and the western sea; the handbooks register the reading without making it doctrine. Cultural legacy: Balor entered the modern world through two doors. The first was scholarship: Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried the sling-stone and the tower into English reading, and O'Rahilly's Early Irish History and Mythology (1946) made him the type-case of the Irish death-king, a scholarly afterlife as large as his medieval dossier is short. The second was the folklore itself: the Donegal oral versions — the tower, the stolen cow, the child cast into the sea — were collected in the nineteenth century and never stopped being retold, and 'Balor of the Evil Eye' remains the standing name of the figure in Irish and in English. In the modern imagination he has become the Celtic dark lord par excellence: the remote tyrant in his island fortress whose one weapon poisons everything it touches, answered not by a greater weapon but by the prophesied grandchild the fortress was built to prevent. Tory Island keeps his address; the Irish language never lost his name. Extended meditation: Every part of Balor's story is about containment failing. The eye is contained — cloaked, lidded, lifted only by machinery — and containment is the whole catastrophe: a gaze so dangerous it must be operated by four other men is no longer a weapon but an occupation, a king reduced to the caretaker of his own poison. The daughter is contained in a tower against a prophecy, and the tower is the prophecy's instrument: no tower, no Cian, no Lugh. Balor is the tradition's purest study of power that can only destroy — he is given no craft, no counsel, no feast, no children worth the having, nothing but the eye and the tax it enforces. And the answer the tradition gives him is exact. Not a bigger eye, not a stronger king, but a sling-stone: small, aimed, and thrown by the one hand the whole machinery existed to forestall. The venom that could wither an army is turned in a single instant into the Fomorians' own epitaph — it was his own host that looked into it. That is the Irish judgment on the evil eye, and on every power built to wither rather than to make: it ends by looking inward. The grandson does not defeat the weapon. He simply turns it around. Original script note: The normalized Old Irish form is Balor — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: balor.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Giant, Brother of Suttungr
text: Giant, Brother of Suttungr: The Keeper of the Door at Hnitbjǫrg Baugi is the giant who holds the one door that matters in the story of the mead of poetry: brother to Suttungr, who hoards the mead inside the mountain Hnitbjǫrg, and master of the nine thralls whose deaths open the way to Óðinn's bargain. He is the hinge of the whole theft — the labour-contractor, the reluctant accomplice, and the would-be cheat whose auger-stroke misses a snake by an inch. Hnitbjǫrg: The mountain — its name plausibly 'the clashing rocks' — inside which Suttungr shut the mead of poetry, with his daughter Gunnlǫð set to guard it. Baugi's auger makes the only door it ever had. Rati: The auger Óðinn puts in Baugi's hands — 'the traveller', from the verb rata. Baugi bores the tunnel with it, and nearly ends the story with one stroke of it. The Whetstone: The sharpening stone Óðinn tosses among Baugi's nine mowing thralls; in scrambling to claim it they cut each other's throats, and Baugi is left with a harvest and no hands. The Mead of Poetry: Kvasir's blood brewed with honey, held in Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són — the drink that makes a poet or a sage of whoever tastes it, and the prize the whole bargain is for. Symbols: Hnitbjǫrg — The mountain of the mead — hoard and fortress in one, opened by craft rather than force; Rati — The auger that gnaws through stone — the tool that makes the door, and nearly the weapon that closes the story; The whetstone — Óðinn's thrown bait — the small object whose coveting empties Baugi's fields of nine workers at a stroke; The nine thralls' scythes — The harvest-tools honed too well — honest labour's edge turned into mutual death by one act of sharpening; Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són — The three vessels of the mead — 'heart-stirrer', 'vessel', and 'reconciliation' — emptied in three draughts Baugi's entire mythology is one episode, and it is the most consequential single episode in the mythology of poetry: the mead heist of Skáldskaparmál. He appears only there and in the þulur of giant-names — a figure the tradition needed once, at the one door, and never again. But that once is the door through which all skaldic poetry claims to have come. Skáldskaparmál: The Mead Comes to Hnitbjǫrg The story begins before Baugi enters it. From the peace-making of Æsir and Vanir is made Kvasir, wisest of beings; the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar kill him and brew his blood with honey into a mead that makes a poet or a scholar of whoever drinks it, keeping it in three vessels — Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són. The dwarfs then drown the giant Gilling at sea and kill his wife with a millstone, and Gilling's son Suttungr takes revenge: he sets the dwarfs on a tide-washed skerry, and they buy their lives with the mead. Suttungr carries it home, shuts it inside the mountain Hnitbjǫrg, and sets his daughter Gunnlǫð to guard it. Only now does Snorri bring Baugi on stage, in a single sentence of genealogy: Suttungr had a brother, and his name was Baugi. The hoard is sealed, the guard is set, and the god who wants the mead does not go to its owner — he goes to the owner's brother. Skáldskaparmál: The Whetstone and the Nine Thralls Óðinn comes walking to Baugi's land calling himself Bǫlverkr, 'Evil-doer' — a name that is not a disguise so much as an announcement. Nine of Baugi's thralls are mowing hay. Bǫlverkr offers to sharpen their scythes, and the whetstone he pulls from his cloak hones so well that all nine want to buy it. He says it will be sold dearly, and throws it up among them; in the scramble to catch it, each thrall swings his scythe at another's neck, and all nine lie dead in the field. That evening Bǫlverkr lodges with Baugi, and Baugi pours out his troubles: his nine thralls are dead and the hay harvest stands uncut. The god has engineered the vacancy he is about to fill — the labour shortage is the lock, and he made it himself. Skáldskaparmál: Nine Men's Work for One Draught Bǫlverkr makes the offer: he will do the work of nine men through the summer, and his wage is one drink of Suttungr's mead. Baugi is careful here, and Snorri gives him the one honest line in the story: he answers that the mead is not his to give — Suttungr alone has control of it — but he will go with Bǫlverkr and they will try together whether they can get it. The bargain is struck: a summer's labour against a hope, with Baugi as broker. Bǫlverkr does the work of nine all summer. When winter comes they go to Suttungr and Baugi puts the case — and Suttungr refuses flatly: not one drop of the mead. Baugi's brokerage has failed on its stated terms; what remains is the attempt he half-promised, the trying of stratagems. Skáldskaparmál: Rati and the Two Blowings Bǫlverkr now asks Baugi for other ways in, and produces the auger called Rati. Baugi bores into the mountain, and says the hole is through. Bǫlverkr leans down and blows into the bore — and the stone-chips fly back into his face. He knows then, Snorri says, that Baugi meant to betray him: the hole is blind. Baugi bores again, and this time when Bǫlverkr blows, the chips fly inward and away. The tunnel is through. Bǫlverkr turns himself into a snake and crawls into the hole — and Baugi strikes after him with the auger, and misses. It is the story's tightest instant: the accomplice becomes the assassin at the threshold, and the mead of all poetry hangs on one failed stroke. Inside waits Gunnlǫð; Óðinn lies with her three nights, wins leave for three draughts, and empties Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són entire. Then he rises as an eagle with all the mead in him, Suttungr in eagle-shape hard behind, and the Æsir set out their vats in Ásgarðr's court — Baugi's door standing open in the mountain behind them all. Hávamál 104–110: Óðinn's Own Version Hávamál lets Óðinn boast of the same theft in his own voice, and the differences are instructive. The god names Rati — 'Rati's mouth I made room for me, and it gnawed the rock' — names Gunnlǫð and the golden seat, names Óðrœrir come up among the Æsir. He names Suttungr defrauded of his mead and Gunnlǫð left weeping, and he names the instrument of it: the baugeiðr, the ring-oath Óðinn swore and broke — 'who can trust him?' But Hávamál never names Baugi. In the god's own telling, the brother at the door has already vanished — the contract, the auger, the missed stroke, all absorbed into Óðinn's solitary cunning. Snorri's prose preserves what the god's boasting omits: that the door had a keeper, that the keeper had a price, and that the keeper tried, at the last moment, to close it on the snake. Syncretism: Baugi himself has no cross-border reflex — no Old English or continental cognate figure, no cult, no charm; he is a person the Icelandic tradition made for one narrative. The myth he serves, however, sits in one of the oldest comparative dossiers in Indo-European study: the theft of the divine intoxicant. The standard parallel is Vedic — the śyena, the eagle or falcon who snatches the soma and brings it to the gods (Rigveda 4.26–27) — set beside Óðinn in eagle-shape carrying off the mead in his body. The comparison was drawn in the nineteenth century and is still registered, with due caution, in the modern handbooks: Lindow treats the mead myth as the northern member of a genuine inheritance while warning against flattening its specifically Norse machinery — the labour contract, the auger, the broken oath. Baugi's own role belongs to that northern machinery: the intermediary who can be bought, the door that opens from the inside. His closest structural kin in the corpus are the other giants whose households Óðinn penetrates by guile, above all the world of [[suttungr|Suttungr]] itself and the deep giant-lore of [[ymir|Ymir]]'s kin. Cultural legacy: Baugi's afterlife is mostly the afterlife of the drink he failed to keep. Skaldic poetry — the entire court-poetry tradition of the Viking and medieval North — called itself by kennings drawn from this myth: Kvasir's blood, the dwarfs' drink, Suttungr's mead, Óðinn's theft, Óðrœrir's wave. Every one of those names is a character in the heist except its doorkeeper; the corpus never minted a 'Baugi's mead'. He survives instead as the specialists' hinge-figure: every scholarly treatment of the mead myth, from Finnur Jónsson to Lindow, must reckon with his two functions — the labour-broker who makes the theft logistically possible, and the wavering accomplice whose bore-hole and auger-stroke are the story's closest brush with failure. In modern retellings of the myth he appears under his name in the better handbooks and in the illustrated Eddas of the Norse revival, always in the same posture: halfway through the mountain, one hand on the auger. The mead myth itself has become the North's great parable of inspiration as something stolen, hoarded, and re-stolen — and the god of poetry, [[bragi|Bragi]], pours out what Baugi could not guard. Extended meditation: Baugi is the indispensable man nobody remembers. Strip him out and the myth stops cold: without the thralls' deaths there is no vacancy, without the contract there is no access, without the auger in his hand there is no door, and without the door there is no mead — and without the mead, by the tradition's own accounting, there is no poetry at all. Yet he is not a hero of his one story, nor even its villain; he is something rarer in the giant-world of the Eddas, a middleman. He names the limits of his power honestly — the mead is Suttungr's, not mine — and then sells access to what is not his anyway. He helps bore the hole and then tries to kill what crawls through it. The tradition leaves his motives exactly that tangled, and the tangle is the point: every hoard is opened from the inside, by someone whose loyalty is a price rather than a fact. The auger-stroke misses by the width of a snake, and because it misses, poems exist. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Baugi — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛒᛅᚢᚴᛁ (b-au-k-i, the k-rune ᚴ writing the g and no rune marking the medial fricative the manuscript spelling preserves). Because the name is pure ASCII, its .com address was registered in the ordinary way and is held outside the PuniCodex collection : no form of the name is currently owned, the plain-ASCII domain is watched for release, and this temple claims none.

title: Knight, One-handed
text: Knight, One-handed: The One-Handed Spearman of Arthur's War-Band Bedwyr son of Bedrawc is the great companion-hero of the oldest Welsh Arthurian tradition: the warrior who never shrank from any enterprise on which [[kai|Cei]] was bound, the one-handed spearman whose single thrust made a wound equal to nine, and the one man the triads crown with a battle-diadem above the three they name. Before French romance gave Arthur his Lancelot, the Welsh tradition gave him Bedwyr. The Lance of Nine Wounds: His one strange property in Culhwch ac Olwen: his lance would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances — one arm doing the work of nine. The Battle-Diadem: The triad of the Three Battle-Diademed names Drystan, Hueil, and Cei — then adds that one was battle-diademed above all three: Bedwyr son of Bedrawc. Cavall the Hound: In the hunting of Twrch Trwyth, the greatest boar-hunt in Welsh literature, Bedwyr led Cavall — Arthur's own hound. The Wooden Tweezers: On the summit of Pumlumon he and Cei plucked the beard of Dillus the Bearded alive with wooden tweezers — for dead, the bristles would have been brittle, and no other leash could hold the hound Drudwyn. Symbols: The one-handed lance — A single arm doing the work of nine — prowess measured by what remains, not what is missing; The battle-diadem — The triad's crown above the crowned — the one name set over Drystan, Hueil, and Cei; Cavall, Arthur's hound — The king's own dog entrusted to his hand in the Twrch Trwyth hunt — trust made visible; The wooden tweezers — The impossible instrument for the impossible task — craft serving the quest on Pumlumon; The sword cast back to the water — In the later Malorian tradition, Bedivere is the last knight, who returns Excalibur to the lake — loyalty outliving the kingdom Bedwyr belongs to the oldest stratum of Arthurian tradition: the Welsh heroic material that predates Geoffrey of Monmouth and the whole romance edifice. His dossier is compact and precise — a poem's roster, a tale's three great episodes, two triads — and across all of it one fact never varies: where Cei goes, Bedwyr goes, and the one-handed man is never the lesser of the pair. Pa gŵr? · Black Book of Carmarthen: The War-Band Remembered The poem known from its opening line as Pa gŵr yv y porthaur? — 'What man is the gatekeeper?' — is the oldest Arthurian poem in Welsh: preserved in the thirteenth-century Black Book of Carmarthen, and itself composed perhaps centuries earlier. In it Arthur, halted at a fortress gate by the porter Glewlwyd Gafaelfawr, recites the roll of his companions to win entry, and Bedwyr stands in that roll beside Cei and Arthur's son Llacheu — already, in the earliest witness, one of the names Arthur speaks to prove his company. The poem is fragmentary — it breaks off mid-recitation — but its testimony matters beyond its length: it shows a Welsh Arthurian war-band whose heroes had their own deeds long before Geoffrey of Monmouth drew Arthur into Latin history, and Bedwyr is fixed in that founding generation.
