The most consequential family in Welsh prose walks the stage under her name, and she never once walks it herself. Math fab Mathonwy: Arianrhod ferch Dôn and the Wand When Math needs a new footholder after Goewin, Gwydion proposes his own sister: 'Seek for you a maiden... here is Arianrhod daughter of Dôn.' The maiden is summoned and asked if she is a virgin; she answers that she does not know but believes she is. Math makes her step over his magic wand, and as she steps she drops a fine yellow-haired boy — Dylan, who at once makes for the sea and takes the sea's nature, Dylan Eil Ton, son of the wave — and, all but unnoticed, 'something small' that only Gwydion marks, wraps in a cloth, and hides in a chest at the foot of his bed. From the chest comes the boy who will be Lleu. Arianrhod, shamed before the whole court, refuses the boy and lays upon him the three tynghedau — the fated destinies — that he shall have no name until she names him, no arms until she arms him, and no wife of any race then on earth. The rest of the branch is Gwydion undoing his sister's curses by craft. Dôn's daughter is the Fourth Branch's proudest and most wounded figure — and Dôn is present, once again, only in the patronymic: uerch Dôn , daughter of Dôn. Culhwch ac Olwen: The Ploughman and the Smith The oldest of the Arthurian tales sends Culhwch to win Olwen, daughter of the chief giant Ysbaddaden Bencawr, who answers the suit by naming the anoethau — the long roll of impossible tasks the suitor must perform before any wedding. Two of Dôn's sons stand inside that list, because the tasks cannot be done without them. Amaethon fab Dôn must be fetched to till the giant's ground: no ploughman alive can work that land but him. And Gofannon fab Dôn, the smith of the divine house, must be brought to the work of the headlands — the craft that prepares the ground is his. The passage is the Welsh tradition's clearest statement of what the Children of Dôn are: not a royal house in the ordinary sense but a house of powers — enchantment, the plough, the forge — each child a function the world cannot do without. Agriculture and smithcraft, the two oldest arts of civilization, belong to the matriarch's sons. Welsh Triads / Kat Godeu: The Futile Battle The Welsh triads keep a battle for the house of Dôn. Among the Three Futile Battles of the Island of Britain stands Cad Goddeu, the Battle of the Trees, fought — the triad says — on account of a bitch, a roebuck, and a lapwing that Amathaon fab Dôn brought away from Annwn, the Otherworld. A theft of three creatures, and a war. The Book of Taliesin's poem Kat Godeu remembers the same war from the other side of the family: it is Gwydion who enchants the trees of the forest into an army — alder at the front, oak in the thick of it — against Arawn of Annwn. One son's theft begins the quarrel, another son's enchantment fights it; and behind both, again, the mother who gives the house its name and never raises a hand in it. The Welsh Genealogies: Plant Dôn Welsh tradition organized its divine and heroic world by the mother's name. Plant Dôn , the Children of Dôn, stands beside Plant Llŷr as one of the two great kindreds of the Mabinogi world, and the genealogical tracts give the matriarch a lineage: Dôn daughter of Mathonwy — which makes her sister to Math fab Mathonwy and explains why her children move so freely in his court. The name-list of her children runs across the sources: Gwydion, Gilfaethwy, and Arianrhod in the Fourth Branch; Gofannon and Amaethon in Culhwch ac Olwen. Later genealogies lengthen the list and supply what the tales omit — a husband, Beli Mawr — but the Mabinogi itself gives Dôn neither husband nor a single word of speech. She is the only major figure of the Four Branches who never appears, and the only one whose name all the others carry. The house is hers because the names are hers; nothing more was ever written, and nothing more was needed. Syncretism: Dôn's great comparison is Irish, and it is as old as modern Celtic studies: [[danu|Danu]] (or Dana), the equally shadowy mother after whom the Túatha Dé Danann — the peoples of the goddess Danu — are named. A Welsh divine kindred called the Children of Dôn and an Irish one called the peoples of Danu look like two faces of one inheritance, and MacKillop and Koch both register the comparison as standard. But it is a comparison, not an equation: no Welsh text identifies the two names, and the philology is genuinely disputed. The traditional reading derives Dôn from Common Celtic *dēwā , 'goddess' — the very word the Welsh language keeps in Dyfrdwy, its name for the River Dee — while a river-name origin, matching the continental Dānuvius (Danube) and the English Don, is also argued; the handbooks leave the question open rather than resolve it. Inside the Welsh corpus her closest kin are the tradition's other mothers and queens: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], the Great Queen of Dyfed, and, in later genealogical speculation, her pairing with [[beli|Beli Mawr]] as father of her children — a marriage the genealogies assert and the Mabinogi never mentions. Her husbandless, speechless sovereignty has no exact parallel anywhere in Celtic literature: she is the matriarch reduced to pure name. Cultural legacy: Dôn rode into English on the same wagon as the rest of the Mabinogi: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation (1838–49) first carried the Fourth Branch into print, and the antiquarian mythography that followed made Plant Dôn the standard label for the northern divine kindred — the house of Gwydion, set beside the house of Llŷr, in every Victorian account of the Welsh gods. Twentieth-century scholarship fixed her place with precision: Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) established the text, Mac Cana's The Mabinogi read the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of Welsh prose, and the great encyclopedias — Koch's Celtic Culture and MacKillop's Dictionary — gave the matriarch her standing head-words, Danu comparison and all. Her widest modern audience came through a children's classic: Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain (1964–68) made 'the Sons of Don' the ruling house of Prydain, with Math son of Mathonwy and Prince Gwydion at Caer Dathyl — her name on the throne of the best-loved Welsh-derived fantasy ever written. Modern Druid and pagan practice honours her as the Welsh mother-goddess and mother of the magical line, and the Welsh sky keeps her children's names: Caer Gwydion, the Milky Way, and Caer Arianrhod among the stars. Extended meditation: Dôn is the matriarch who never speaks. Every other great figure of the Four Branches is given a scene, a speech, a deed — Gwydion his enchantments, Arianrhod her curses, Math his wand — and Dôn is given nothing but the space before her children's names. Yet the whole architecture of the tale leans on that silence: the northern house of Welsh mythology is not the house of Mathonwy her father, or of Math her brother, but the Children of Dôn , the kindred named for the mother. The sources are telling us something about where authority lived in the world behind the tales — that the line itself could be reckoned through the woman, and the name that organized a pantheon could be hers alone. Her restoration is like her: three plain letters, hidden in plain sight. Don is an English word, an English river, a Spanish title — and underneath all of them the Welsh mother of gods, carrying a name the tradition glossed as 'goddess' itself. The project rescues diacritics from the address bar; it cannot rescue a scene the manuscripts never wrote. What it can do, and does here, is keep the mother-name at the head of the house, spelled exactly as the White Book and the Red Book spell it, and say plainly what the record is: a goddess made of her children's names, and a name made of nothing but itself. Original script note: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Don — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1375–1420), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Modern Welsh orthography writes Dôn with a circumflex, but that mark is a modern length-sign for the long vowel, not a letter any manuscript carries; the project therefore follows the manuscript form, and the name stands in Tier 2 by the mechanical rule — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, nothing for ASCII to lose. Because the name is pure ASCII — and also an ordinary English word and river-name — its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: don.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/don/ in the meantime.

title: Odin's Ring, Wealth
text: Odin's Ring, Wealth: The Dripper of the Ninth Night Draupnir is the golden arm-ring of Óðinn, forged by the dwarf Sindri while his brother Brokkr worked the bellows — the one treasure in the northern corpus that increases by its own nature. Every ninth night eight new rings of equal weight drip from it, so that the Allfather's wealth is not a hoard but a fountain. Óðinn laid it on Baldr's pyre as his last gift to his son, and Baldr sent it back from Hel with Hermóðr: the ring that crosses the boundary of death in both directions. Sindri's Forge: The dwarf-smith's hearth where gold went in and the ring came out — Brokkr at the bellows, forbidden to stop, and a fly on his hand. The Eight Rings: Every ninth night, eight rings of equal weight drip from the one — wealth that multiplies in the dark, without labour and without theft. Baldr's Pyre: The ring Óðinn laid on Hringhorni's fire beside his dead son — the father's parting gift, sent into the smoke with the fairest of the Æsir. Hermóðr's Return: The token Baldr sent back from Hel's hall with the nine-night rider — proof, in gold, that the errand reached the dead god's hand. Symbols: The gold ring itself — Wealth that breeds wealth — the one treasure in the corpus whose nature is increase, not keeping; The ninth night — The interval of multiplication — eight rings of equal weight for every nine nights the ring is kept; Brokkr's bellows — The unbroken breath of the forge — the wager turned on a blast no fly could interrupt twice; The fly (Loki) — The sting that cost the hammer its handle but could not touch the ring — malice spent against patience; The pyre-token — The gift that goes down with the dead and returns with the messenger — love's keepsake across Hel's gate Draupnir's dossier divides cleanly in two: Skáldskaparmál tells its making, in the wager that also produced Gullinbursti and Mjǫllnir, and the Baldr cycle tells its journey — into the fire with the dead god and back out of Hel with the living one's token. Between those poles the Poetic Edda catches it twice: offered and refused in Skírnismál, and catalogued as a dwarf's own name in Völuspá. Skáldskaparmál: The Wager of Loki's Head It begins with a crime of Loki's: he cut off all the hair of Sif, Þórr's wife, for mischief. Þórr caught him and would have broken every bone in him, but Loki swore to get the black-elves to make Sif hair of gold that would grow like other hair. He went to the dwarfs called the sons of Ivaldi, and they made the golden hair, and Skíðblaðnir, the best of ships, for Freyr, and the spear Gungnir for Óðinn. Then Loki boasted, and his boasting made the bet: he wagered his own head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Sindri could not make three treasures as good as these. Snorri frames the whole episode as an explanation of how the gods got their treasures — the myth exists in the Edda to account for the properties of the great objects, and Draupnir's property is the strangest of them: it does not merely exist; it multiplies. Skáldskaparmál: Three Treasures from the Bellows Sindri laid a pig's skin in the forge and told Brokkr to blow, and never to stop until he himself drew the work out. When the smith had gone from the forge, a fly settled on Brokkr's hand and stung him — but he blew on. Out came the boar with bristles of gold, Gullinbursti. Next Sindri laid gold in the forge and gave the same command; the fly settled on Brokkr's neck and stung twice as hard — but he blew on. Out came the ring Draupnir. Last came iron, and the fly settled between Brokkr's eyes and stung the eyelid until blood ran down and blinded him; he swept the fly away with his hand, and for that one moment the bellows failed — and so the hammer Mjǫllnir came out with its handle too short. The fly was Loki, spending himself against the bellows. The brothers carried the three treasures to Ásgarðr to be judged against Loki's three. Óðinn received the spear Gungnir and the ring Draupnir, and Snorri gives the ring's nature in a single sentence the whole tradition repeats: every ninth night, eight rings of equal weight drip from it. Freyr took the ship and the boar; Þórr took the hammer. The Æsir judged Mjǫllnir the best of all, because it was the surest defence against the rime-giants — but Loki kept his head on a point of law: Brokkr might have the head, but not one hair of the neck. So the dwarf sewed Loki's lips shut instead, and the wager closed with the gods six treasures richer. Skírnismál 21–22: The Ring Refused The Poetic Edda catches the ring in motion, being offered as a bride-price. When Freyr's servant Skírnir rides to Jötunheimr to woo the giant's daughter Gerðr for his lovesick master, he carries gifts, and the second of them is the ring: 'the ring that was burned with Óðinn's young son; eight of equal weight drip from it every ninth night.' The poem does not name it — it does not need to; no other ring in the corpus matches the description, and the tradition from the prose commentators onward has read it as Draupnir. Gerðr refuses it: she wants no gold, she says, for she lacks none in her father Gymir's halls, and will not share wealth with Freyr's messenger. The episode is a quiet marvel of the corpus: the self-breeding ring of the Allfather, the one gift that cannot be outbid, laid before a giantess who counts it worthless. Only Skírnir's curse, carved in runes and threats, moves her where Óðinn's treasure could not — the poem's own verdict that gold, even multiplying gold, buys nothing that matters. Gylfaginning 49: The Ring on the Pyre When Baldr lay dead of the mistletoe and the Æsir built his pyre on Hringhorni, the greatest of ships, the funeral gathered the whole wealth of the gods' grief. Nanna died of sorrow at the sight of him and was laid beside her husband; Þórr hallowed the pyre with Mjǫllnir; and Óðinn did the thing this temple exists to record: he laid the ring Draupnir on the fire with his son. No word of his is preserved with the gift. The dripper, the fountain of the Allfather's gold, went into the smoke as a father's last giving to the child he could not keep. The corpus keeps the gesture where it belongs — among the funeral's few named acts, beside the hallowing hammer and the burst heart. A ring that makes eight more of itself every ninth night is the least losable treasure in the world, and Óðinn loses it deliberately, which is exactly what makes it a gift. Gylfaginning 49 · Völuspá: Back from Hel, and the Dwarf's Name The story does not let the ring rest in the fire. Hermóðr the Bold rode nine nights down the dark road, leapt Helgrindr on Sleipnir, and found Baldr seated in the high seat of Hel's hall. When Hel set her famous condition — that all things in the world must weep Baldr out — Baldr sent tokens home with the rider, and first among them was Draupnir, returned to Óðinn as a keepsake. The ransom failed at Þökk's one refusal, and Baldr stayed with the dead; but the ring came back across the boundary that nothing else crosses, carrying the dead god's love to the living father. It is the only object in the corpus to make that journey in both directions. Völuspá preserves the name's older, stranger root: in the dvergatal, the great catalogue of dwarfs, a dwarf named Draupnir stands in the list beside Dólgþrasir and his kin. The treasure-name and the dwarf-name are the same word — 'the dripper' — and scholars have long noted how naturally the corpus names its wonders after its smiths. The ring that drips gold wears a name the dwarf-lists already owned, as if the Edda kept, fossilized in its oldest poem, the memory that such things come from under the earth. Syncretism: Draupnir needs no borrowed god to explain it — it is an object, and its company is other objects. The corpus itself sets the sharpest contrast: [[andvari|Andvari]]'s ring Andvaranaut, extorted at the waterfall and cursed, kills every hand that holds it, while Draupnir, freely made for the gods on a wager's terms, breeds gold for its keeper — the taken ring destroys, the given ring multiplies. The wider Germanic context is the ring-giving culture the poetry everywhere assumes: Beowulf's lord is the *beaga brytta*, the 'ring-giver', and arm-rings were the very currency of loyalty between lord and man; a self-breeding ring is that economy's dream made metal. Folklorists file Draupnir among the self-multiplying magic treasures of the international motif-index, beside inexhaustible purses and cornucopias; its nearest mythic cousins are things, not gods. Within the corpus its makers [[brokkr|Brokkr]] and [[sindri|Sindri]] and its fellow-wonders — Gullinbursti, and [[thor|Þórr]]'s hammer [[mjolnir|Mjǫllnir]] from the same forging — are its true kin. Cultural legacy: Draupnir's afterlife is the afterlife of an idea: the treasure that makes treasure. Nineteenth-century retellings fixed the forging-wager as a set-piece of the Norse revival — the Kearys' The Heroes of Asgard (1857) carries Brokkr and Sindri at the bellows, and every handbook since repeats the ninth-night dripping. In modern popular culture the name has become a byword for self-replicating wonders: God of War Ragnarök (2022) gives Brok and Sindri a Draupnir of its own — a spear, forged from the ring's multiplying magic, that reproduces itself in the wielder's hand — the most widely seen adaptation of the dwarf-brothers and their craft in any medium. Fantasy games and fiction reach for the name whenever gear must breed gear. In Iceland the word never needed reviving: Draupnir remains a living name there for ships, firms, and horses, the dripper doing ordinary work in the language that wrote the Eddas. And every time a modern storyteller needs wealth that grows honestly — by time, by patience, by nature rather than by taking — the shape they reach for is Óðinn's ring, whether they name it or not. Extended meditation: The North was not sentimental about gold. Its greatest hoard is cursed at birth, its dragons die on their beds of metal, and its poets ken gold as the fire of the flood where the Niflungar sank it. Against all of that stands one exception, and it is the highest treasure of the highest god: a ring whose only property is that it increases. Draupnir does not shine, speak, strike, or protect. It drips — on a schedule, in the dark, eight for one every ninth night, wealth arriving the way wealth actually arrives for those who keep it lawfully: slowly, cyclically, and by nature rather than by conquest. The myth then does the two most instructive things a myth can do with such an object. It gives it away: Óðinn lays the one inexhaustible treasure in the world on his son's pyre, because no fountain of gold outweighs one act of love. And it sends it back: the dead return the gift to the living, because some bonds outlast the boundary. Between those two gestures the ring becomes something stranger than a treasure — a measure of what treasure is for. The cursed ring of the dwarf [[andvari|Andvari]] passes from hand to hand and each owner dies; the dripper passes from father to son and back to father, and the only thing that multiplies is the meaning. Gold that is kept breeds gold. Gold that is given breeds everything else. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Draupnir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛏᚱᛅᚢᛒᚾᛁᛦ (t-r-au-b-n-i-R, the ᛏ-rune writing d, ᛒ writing p, and ᛦ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: draupnir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: The Water Horse of the Lochs
text: The Water Horse of the Lochs: The Perfect Stallion, the Adhesive Back, and the Liver That Floated Ashore Eachuisge — the each-uisge, the water horse — is the most dangerous being in the Highland Otherworld: a shape-shifter that haunts the lochs and sea-lochs of Gaelic Scotland, wearing the shape of a flawless stallion at the water's edge. Mount him and your hands stick fast to his hide; the loch does the rest. The Lowland kelpie haunts rivers and is content to drown you — the each-uisge devours. The Loch: His true country: the deep freshwater lochs and sea-lochs of the Highlands, where he waits beneath the surface. The Perfect Stallion: His chosen lure: a beautiful horse standing tame by the shore, offered to any traveler in a hurry. The Adhesive Back: Once mounted, the rider cannot dismount: the hide holds the hand like pitch, and the horse runs for the water. The Handsome Stranger: His other shape: a fine young man by the shore — betrayed, the tales say, by the water-weed in his hair. Symbols: The flawless stallion — The too-perfect gift at the water's edge — beauty as bait, offered where the ground runs out; The adhesive hide — The choice that cannot be unmade: once mounted, the mount decides; The liver on the shore — The one thing the loch gives back — the Highland record's grimmest detail, and its proof that this horse devours; The weed in the stranger's hair — The tell the shape cannot shed: water keeps its mark on whatever walks out of it The each-uisge has no medieval manuscript behind him: his mythology is oral, and its primary witnesses are the great nineteenth-century field collections of the Highlands — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland. The tales agree on the essentials with the consistency of a warning passed from shore to shore. Highland oral tradition: The Rider Taken The core of every telling is the same. A traveler on the shore of a loch finds a beautiful horse standing idle — fine beyond any horse in the parish, saddled by luck, or so it seems. He mounts; the horse is smooth and willing; and then the rider finds his hands fast to the hide, stuck as if with bird-lime, and the horse's head already turned toward the water. The loch takes them both. In the grimmest tellings the loch gives the rider back in pieces — the tradition is exact about this: the each-uisge devours the whole body, and what floats ashore is the liver alone. That detail is the Highland folklore's way of drawing the line between its own water horse and the Lowland kelpie, which drowns but does not eat. Highland oral tradition: The Boy Who Cut Off His Finger The best-known of the warning-tales gives the creature a longer game. A fine horse appears to children playing by a loch, and one by one they climb its back — and the back lengthens to take them, seat after seat, until all are mounted save one wary boy, who will only touch the hide with a finger. The horse springs for the water with its load of children, and the boy, stuck by that single finger, does the one thing left: he cuts the finger off and escapes. The loch gives back the others the next day, piecemeal. The collectors recorded the tale across the Highlands, and Briggs notes it among the each-uisge's defining episodes: the compound's lesson compressed into a single image — touch with everything and you lose everything; touch with a finger and a finger pays for the lesson. Highland oral tradition: The Handsome Stranger The horse is only the working shape. The each-uisge also walks ashore as a fine young man, and the tales of the loch-side courting are as consistent as the tales of the ride. A girl meets a handsome stranger by the water; he lays his head in her lap and sleeps; and as she combs his hair with her fingers she finds in it the sand and weed of the loch bottom. She understands what is sleeping on her knee, eases her skirt free, and runs — and behind her the shape comes apart into horse and water. The weed in the hair is the tradition's signature: the shape-shifter can borrow any face but cannot shed the mark of the element he came from. Highland oral tradition: The Red-Hot Iron The record also remembers that the each-uisge can be killed, and how. Ordinary iron and ordinary courage fail against a thing that lives in the water; the answer the tales keep is fire carried into iron. In the well-known Highland account preserved by John Gregorson Campbell, a smith destroys a water horse with a red-hot iron — a spear or bar heated in the forge and driven home while the creature is held fast. The pattern is the old one the collectors noted across Gaelic tradition: the supernatural yields to the smith, whose craft joins the two elements the water horse cannot master — fire, and the metal that remembers it. The tale matters to the record because it is nearly unique: almost everything else the Highlands says about the each-uisge is a way to avoid him. Syncretism: The each-uisge is the Highland head of a family that runs the length of the Celtic coasts and beyond. His closest cousin is the Lowland Scots kelpie , which haunts rivers rather than lochs and is generally the milder power — drowning without devouring; the two are kindred, not cognate, for the words are unrelated. The Northern Isles keep their own: Shetland's nuggle or njogel, and Orkney's nuckelavee , a far worse thing — a skinless fusion of man and horse that must be distinguished from the shape-shifting water horse proper. The Isle of Man has the cabbyl-ushtey, Wales the ceffyl dŵr, and Ireland the each-uisce and the shape-shifting [[pooka|Púca]], which takes horse-shape among its many forms. The tradition is older than the collections: [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]]'s horse Aonbharr, which runs over land and sea alike, shows the medieval Irish imagination already at work on the horse that owns both elements. Beyond the Celtic world the type recurs — the Scandinavian bäckahäst and the nøkk among them — and the handbooks treat the whole complex as one of the most widespread figure-types of northern European water-lore: the horse as the beautiful face of drowning. Cultural legacy: The each-uisge entered print through the great Victorian field collections — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860–62) and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900) — and it never left. Katharine Briggs's Encyclopedia of Fairies fixed its modern profile as the fiercest of the British water-horses, and MacKillop's Dictionary of Celtic Mythology carried it into the standard Celtic reference shelf. Burns had already put the Lowland cousin into verse — the 'water-kelpie' of the Address to the Deil — and the whole water-horse tradition stands behind the Highlands' most famous modern legend: commentators have long read the loch-monster lore of the twentieth century against this older record of horses in the water. Andy Scott's Kelpies at Falkirk (2013), the thirty-meter horse-head sculptures on the Forth and Clyde Canal, are the tradition's monumental afterlife — kelpies by name, but the image they make permanent is the each-uisge's own: the horse rising out of Scottish water. In Gaelic itself the compound never went anywhere: each-uisge still means the water horse, and the warning it carries is older than any collection that preserves it. Extended meditation: The each-uisge is the most honest monster in the Celtic record, because its method is consent. It does not chase, does not strike, does not break down any door. It stands at the water's edge in the shape of the one thing a tired traveler most wants — a beautiful horse, unclaimed, waiting — and it lets the victim do the approaching. Everything that follows follows from a single step: the moment of mounting. After that there is no further decision to make, and that is the horror the Highland tellers kept sharpening — the adhesive hide, the back that lengthens to take one more, the hands that will not come free. The tradition is not superstition in the cheap sense; it is risk assessment in story form. Water in the Highlands is deep, cold, and patient, and the loch that will drown you looks exactly like the loch that will carry your boat. The each-uisge personifies that double face: the surface that offers itself and the depth that keeps what it takes. And its one consistent weakness is the oldest rule of the shore — touch with a finger first, and be ready to lose the finger rather than the rest. Original script note: The name is the ordinary Gaelic common-noun compound each-uisge , 'water horse', written in the Latin alphabet Gaelic has used since the early medieval period — normalized here as Eachuisge for the temple form. There is no older monumental attestation: the figure belongs to oral tradition, and its primary record is the nineteenth-century field collection, not the manuscript codex. The compound is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — so the restoration changes nothing but the capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: eachuisge.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Knowledge, Wisdom
text: Knowledge, Wisdom: The Poet of the Hidden Meanings; the Sense That Can Be Taken but Not Held Écne is Old Irish for knowledge itself — and the name of the wisdom of the Túatha Dé Danann made personal: a poet of the divine race whose dossier is a single luminous word and a place on the list. Around the name the Irish learned tradition built its whole physics of wisdom: nine hazels over the well, nuts of knowledge falling into the water, and the salmon that feeds on them — sense that can be tasted, carried, and passed on, but never dammed or owned. The Nine Hazels: The hazels of wisdom stood over the well in the Otherworld, blossoming and fruiting in a single hour, dropping their nuts into the water below. The Well of Wisdom: Connla's well, the well of Segais — the hidden source beneath the hazels, from which the rivers of knowledge flow and to which none may walk who is not called. The Salmon of Knowledge: The fish that feeds on the fallen nuts and wears their wisdom as spots — knowledge that must be caught, cooked, and tasted, never kept. Imbas, the Great Knowledge: The poet's illumination — the flash of knowing that comes unbidden, burns the thumb that touches it first, and belongs to no one for long. Symbols: The nine hazels of wisdom — Wisdom drops its fruit into the water, not into the hand — knowledge comes by its own season, never by demand; The well of Segais / Connla's well — The hidden source under the world-tree's mirror — every stream of knowing traced back to one spring no map holds; The salmon of knowledge — The carrier that feeds on the fallen nuts and wears their marks — sense that can be taken, tasted, and passed on, but not held; The nuts of knowledge — Cormac's Glossary read the very word as 'from nuts' — the medieval tradition's own image of wisdom cracking its shell; Imbas, the great knowledge — The poet's sudden illumination — knowing as an event that happens to a person, not a property a person owns Écne has the thinnest dossier of any figure in this collection — no surviving tale acts him, no epithet colors him, no treasure is laid in his hand. The tradition gives a name, a word, and a seat among the poets of the Túatha Dé Danann, and then it does something stranger and more honest: it tells the myths of the thing the name means. The mythology of Écne is the mythology of knowledge itself — the well, the hazels, the salmon, and everyone who ever burned a thumb on it. eDIL · MacKillop: The Name on the List Old Irish écne — also written eicne — is the common noun for knowledge, wisdom, understanding, the word the glossators reach for when they mean knowing of the deepest kind. The medieval tradition also knew it as a personal name: Écne, a poet of the Túatha Dé Danann, wisdom personified and given a seat among the divine race. That is nearly all that survives — no adventure, no contest, no death-tale. The dictionaries and the handbooks, from the Dictionary of the Irish Language to MacKillop, record the figure and then fall back on the word. The thinness is itself the tradition's comment. Irish myth is lavish with its kings and its cattle-raids, but when it personifies wisdom it falls silent on purpose: the file, the poet, was the one who knew that the highest knowledge does not submit to narrative. Écne stands in the lists the way a word stands in a glossary — complete, and pointing elsewhere. Sanas Cormaic: Knowledge from Nuts Around the year 900, Cormac mac Cuilennáin's glossary — Sanas Cormaic, the first etymological dictionary in any vernacular of western Europe — took the word in hand and explained it in the manner medieval Ireland loved: écne comes from cnú, the nut, for knowledge comes from nuts. Modern philology treats the derivation as learned play rather than history, and the word's deeper etymology remains unsettled. But the gloss was never really about linguistics. It was a compressed myth. Everyone who heard it knew the image the gloss was invoking: the hazels of wisdom and the well beneath them, the nuts that carry knowing in their shells. Cormac's etymology is the tradition folding its whole doctrine of wisdom into a dictionary entry — the sense that knowledge is something grown, ripened, dropped, and only then taken up. The learned tradition: The Well and the Hazels The Irish learned tradition kept the physics of wisdom exact. In the Otherworld stands a well — Connla's well, or the well of Segais — and over it grow the nine hazels of wisdom, which blossom and fruit in a single hour so that flower and nut hang together. The nuts of knowledge fall into the water, and the salmon of the well feed on them, and whoever would drink wisdom must wait for what the trees let fall. The image runs through the medieval teaching tradition and the mythological handbooks that preserve it, and it never varies in its essentials: the source is hidden, the fruit drops on its own season, and the water carries the knowing outward into every river of the world. It is the exact opposite of a treasure-hoard. Wisdom in this tradition is not stored; it flows, and the best any person can do is stand downstream of it. Macgnímartha Finn: The Salmon and the Thumb The tradition's great story of wisdom received belongs to Fionn mac Cumhaill. In the Boyhood Deeds of Finn, the boy — still called Demne — comes to the poet Finnéces, who has waited seven years by the Boyne for the salmon of knowledge, the fish that fed on the nuts of the well. On the day the boy arrives, the salmon is caught at last; Finnéces gives it to Demne to cook, with one command: eat none of it. The boy burns his thumb on the fish and thrusts it into his mouth — and the knowledge that seven years of watching could not win passes into him by accident. When Finnéces asks whether he ate of the salmon, the boy answers no, and tells the truth of the thumb; the poet, who waited longest, surrenders the fish and the gift to him. It is the tradition's perfect parable of its wisdom-word: knowledge is not inherited, purchased, or even earned by patience. It is tasted — and it goes where it will. The Settling of the Manor of Tara: The Salmon That Remembers The oldest bearer of the tradition's knowledge is Fintan mac Bóchra, the survivor who outlived the Flood itself. When the nobles of Ireland disputed the divisions of Tara, the judgment had to be sought from memory deeper than any living man's — and Fintan was found at last, ancient beyond reckoning, having passed through the shapes of salmon, eagle, and hawk, remembering every wave and every king since the waters rose. Fintan settles the manor from the store of what he has witnessed, and the tale makes explicit what the well-and-salmon complex implies: knowledge in the Irish imagination is fundamentally memory — not a set of answers but the long holding of what the world has let fall. Écne's tradition keeps both halves: wisdom flows like water, and yet somewhere, in some salmon of the well, nothing is ever forgotten. Syncretism: Écne has no cross-border attestation — no Gaulish altar, no Welsh namesake, and the handbooks claim none; the figure is Irish through and through, a word given a face. But the pattern the word belongs to crosses the Irish Sea intact. The Welsh tradition keeps its own story of wisdom arriving by accident to the wrong cook: the boy Gwion Bach, set to stir Ceridwen's cauldron of inspiration for a year and a day, takes the three scalding drops of awen meant for her son, and flees through shape after shape until he is reborn as Taliesin, the radiant-browed chief of poets. The parallel with Fionn and the salmon — the helper, the burn, the unmeant gift, the shape-changed transmission — is the standard comparison in the handbooks, and it maps a shared Celtic doctrine: poetic wisdom is a substance that passes from vessel to vessel, and no one can hold it by force. Within the Irish tradition Écne's closest kin are the other masters of knowing: Brigit, whom Cormac's Glossary calls the goddess the poets worshipped; Ogma, the honey-mouthed champion of eloquence; the Dagda, Ruad Rofhessa, the Red One of Great Knowledge; and Fionn himself, the wisdom-taster of the Boyne. Cultural legacy: Écne's afterlife runs through the thing the name means rather than through the name itself. The salmon of knowledge became Ireland's emblem of learning: it crowns the crests of schools and universities, and John Kindness's great ceramic-clad Salmon of Knowledge — the Big Fish of Donegall Quay, Belfast, raised in 1999 — carries the hazel-and-well story in printed tiles across its scales, the most famous piece of public art in the city. The Boyhood Deeds of Finn, with the thumb and the salmon, entered every Irish schoolroom through Lady Gregory's retellings and the Fenian anthologies, so that the parable of wisdom tasted by accident is one of the best-known stories in the language. The old word itself faded from ordinary Irish — eolas and fios do its daily work now — but the learned tradition kept écne in the glossaries, and the revival's scholars, from Kuno Meyer onward, restored the figure to the reference books where it stands today: the Túatha Dé Danann's own personification of the sense that can be taken but not held. Extended meditation: Écne is the god of the thing that slips through the fingers — knowledge as water, as falling fruit, as the fish that must be eaten in the moment or not at all. Every other figure in this collection is measured by what it holds: a hammer, a harp, a hoard, a hall. Écne holds nothing, because the tradition understood that the highest sense cannot be warehoused. The hazels drop their nuts on their own hour; the well gives only to those who stand downstream; the salmon yields its wisdom to the burned thumb of a boy who was told to wait. That is the doctrine's edge, and it has not blunted in twelve centuries. The poet Finnéces kept vigil for seven years and the knowledge went to his kitchen-boy — not as injustice, but as the nature of the gift. What Écne names is the difference between information and understanding: the first can be copied, stored, and owned; the second must happen to you. The word survives in the glossaries like a sign at the head of a river — this way to the water; bring nothing to carry it in. Original script note: The normalized Old Irish form is écne (also spelled eicne in the manuscripts) — Old Irish in the Insular Latin script, with the síneadh fada marking the long é in modern dictionary normalization. Old Irish scribes wrote vowel length inconsistently, and the manuscript spellings are plain; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, predates the manuscript tradition and preserves no attestation of this name. The temple form Ecne follows the unmarked manuscript spelling and is already plain ASCII, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: ecne.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Trouble, Mischief
text: Trouble, Mischief: The Strife-Maker of the Second Branch, and the Cauldron He Died Breaking Efnysien is the destroyer of the Mabinogi: the man the Second Branch introduces in a single balanced sentence — his brother Nisien could make peace between two armies at their most embittered; Efnysien could make two brothers quarrel when they loved each other best. One act of his, the maiming of the Irish king's horses, sets two kingdoms on the road to ruin; his last act, the breaking of the Cauldron of Rebirth, costs him his heart and ends the slaughter he began. The Maimed Horses: At the wedding feast of Aberffraw, in a rage that no one had asked his consent, he cuts the lips, ears, tails, and eyelids of Matholwch's horses — the insult that compensation could not bury. The Cauldron of Rebirth: Pair Dadeni — the vessel Brân gives in compensation: a slain man thrown in today rises tomorrow a fighting man, but speechless. Efnysien dies stretching it to pieces. The Hundred Bags: In the great house the Irish built for Brân, a hundred armed men hide in flour-bags hung on the pillars. Efnysien walks the row, asks what is in each bag, and crushes a skull through the sacking with his fingers. The Boy in the Fire: At the peace feast his nephew Gwern — Branwen's child, newly made king — goes from lap to lap; at Efnysien's lap he is seized and thrown into the flames. After that there is no peace to be made. Symbols: The mutilated horses — Pride made visible — an insult so literal that no payment could make the injured king forget it; The Cauldron of Rebirth (Pair Dadeni) — War stripped of death's limit — the gift that became a weapon, until the one who broke it broke himself; The flour-bags on the pillars — Treachery hidden in hospitality — seen through only by the man whose own mind worked that way; Gwern cast into the flames — The murder of the heir at the moment of his investiture — the point past which the tale permits no return; The broken heart — His only death-wound: he stretched himself inside the cauldron until it burst into four pieces, and his heart broke with it Efnysien belongs to one tale and fills it: the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr. The branch is the story of a compensation that failed, and Efnysien is the reason — twice over the author of the injury, and at the end the author of the only sacrifice that stopped the ruin. Mabinogi, Second Branch: The Two Brothers The tale introduces him by contrast. Penarddun ferch Beli, mother of Brân the Blessed, Branwen, and Manawydan by Llŷr, bore two sons to Euroswydd: Nisien and Efnysien. Of Nisien the branch says he was a good man and a gentle youth, who could bring peace between two armies at their most embittered; of Efnysien it says he would set two brothers at strife when they loved each other most. The whole Second Branch is the working-out of that one sentence. Mabinogi, Second Branch: The Maiming of the Horses When Brân gave his half-sister Branwen to Matholwch, king of Ireland, the wedding feast was held at Aberffraw, and the horses of the Irish king were stabled for the night. Efnysien asked why they were there, and was told they belonged to Matholwch, who had married his sister. 'Is this what they have done with a maiden as fine as her, my own sister — given her away without asking me?' In his rage he went under the horses and cut off their lips to the teeth, their ears to the head, their tails to the rumps, and their eyelids to the bone. Matholwch rose in silence and made for his ships; only Brân's embassy — Manawydan among them — and the offer of honour-price brought him back: a silver staff as tall as himself, a gold plate as broad as his face, fresh horses, and the Cauldron of Rebirth, which Brân had from Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid and Cymidei Cymeinfoll, wanderers who had fled to his court out of Ireland. Mabinogi, Second Branch: The Hundred Bags of Flour The compensation did not hold. In Ireland the insult was remembered, Matholwch was shamed by his own nobles, and Branwen was sent to the kitchen with a box on the ear from the butcher every day — until she tamed a starling and sent word across the sea. Brân waded the channel, for no ship could carry him, and lay across the river when the Irish destroyed the bridge: 'He who would be a leader, let him be a bridge.' The Irish sued for terms: the kingship would pass to Gwern, Branwen's son, and they would build Brân a house great enough to hold him — the first house he had ever entered. But in that house they hung a hundred bags, an armed man in each. Efnysien walked the row ahead of the feast, laid his hand on each bag — 'What is in here?' 'Flour.' — and squeezed each head through the sacking until he felt the skull give, a hundred times down the hall. Mabinogi, Second Branch: The Boy in the Fire At the feast of reconciliation the boy Gwern was invested as king, and — charming everyone, the branch says — he went from lap to lap among his kinsmen, from Brân to Manawydan to Nisien, until he came to Efnysien's lap. 'Why does my nephew not come to me?' Efnysien asked; and when the boy was put into his arms he seized him by the feet and threw him headlong into the great fire. Branwen would have leapt in after her son, but Brân caught her with one hand and took up his shield with the other, and the hall rose in war. It is the tale's darkest sentence, and its hinge: after Gwern, no negotiation is possible. Mabinogi, Second Branch: The Breaking of the Cauldron In the battle that followed, the Irish had the advantage that could not be beaten: every night they cast their slain into the Cauldron of Rebirth, and every morning the dead rose as fighting men again — speechless, but unkillable in any final sense. Then Efnysien, seeing the ruin he had made, did the one thing only he could do. He lay down among the Irish dead as if he were a corpse, was thrown into the cauldron with them, and stretched himself out inside it until the vessel burst into four pieces — and his own heart burst with it, and so he died. The branch gives him no speech of repentance and no eulogy: the destroyer ends the war his own hand started, at the price of his life, and the narration passes on. Of the hosts of Britain only seven men came home, bearing Brân's head; Branwen died of a broken heart on the shore of Anglesey and was buried in a four-sided grave on the bank of the Alaw. Syncretism: The comparison that follows Efnysien everywhere is with [[loki|Loki]]: the malice inside the house, the sworn kin whose mischief costs the gods their peace, the trickster the tale can neither spare nor save. MacKillop and the handbooks register the parallel as typological rather than genealogical — the Mabinogi's strife-maker is a human prince of the Children of Llŷr, not a god, and his story answers to Welsh concerns: the honour-price, the insult remembered, the compensation that fails. The truer Celtic company is the cauldron-complex: the Cauldron of Rebirth belongs to the same deep stock as the Dagda's cauldron from Murias in the Lebor Gabála Érenn, from which no company went away unsatisfied, and the branch itself gives the vessel an Irish provenance through the fugitive Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid. Within the corpus his closest kin are [[nisien|Nisien]], the brother he was written as the opposite of, and [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the king his pride destroyed; [[manawydan|Manawydan]] and [[taliesin|Taliesin]] are among the seven who carried Brân's head home. Cultural legacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried the Second Branch into the English-speaking world, and Efnysien's maiming of the horses and death in the cauldron became set-pieces of the Victorian Celtic revival. Evangeline Walton retold the branch at full length in The Children of Llyr (1971), the second volume of her Mabinogion tetralogy, and gave him the modern novel's inside view without softening him. His widest-reaching legacy is the cauldron itself: Lloyd Alexander drew the deathless cauldron-born warriors of his Prydain chronicles — The Black Cauldron (1965), filmed by Disney in 1985 — directly from the Welsh matter, where a cauldron that returns the slain to silent service is broken at terrible cost. In Welsh memory the branch left two landmarks: the proverb 'A fo ben, bid bont' — he who would be a leader, let him be a bridge — and Bedd Branwen, the grave by the Alaw where the tradition buried the sister his acts helped kill. Extended meditation: Efnysien is what a story looks like when it refuses to flatter anyone — including itself. The Second Branch never explains him. He is not possessed, not wronged first, not mad; the tale simply pairs him with Nisien and lets the contrast stand: what one brother binds, the other unbinds, and the world has both kinds of man in it. His evil is small in scale and total in consequence — a night with a knife in a stable, and two kingdoms bleed for a generation. That is the branch's hardest teaching about trouble: it does not need to be great, only timely, and no compensation is large enough to make an injured king forget. And then the ending, which the Welsh text declines to call redemption. Efnysien sees what his mischief has cost — the speechless dead rising nightly from the cauldron — and lies down among the corpses of the enemy to be thrown in with them. No one forgives him in the text; no one praises him; the branch records only that the cauldron broke and his heart broke. The destroyer is allowed one act of destruction aimed at destruction itself, and it costs exactly everything he has. The Mabinogi does not promise that the man who sets the fire can put it out. It shows him choosing to burn with it. Original script note: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as Efnisien — Middle Welsh (Brythonic Celtic), attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), recording material composed centuries earlier. The normalized form writes plain Latin letters with no diacritic, so the restoration Efnysien differs from the ASCII input only in the capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: efnysien.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Healing, Mercy, Medical Skill
text: Healing, Mercy, Medical Skill: The Best Physician of the Ásynjur Eir is the Norse tradition's one physician: third in Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur, defined by a single superlative — læknir beztr, 'the best of healers' — and named again among the healing maidens of Lyfjaberg in Fjölsvinnsmál. Her name is the common noun for mercy itself. Lyfjaberg: The 'mountain of healing' where Menglöð sits with her maidens — lyf is the Old Norse word for medicinal herbs and remedies. The Nine Maidens: Hlíf, Hlífþursa, Þjóðvarta, Björt, Blíð, Blíðr, Fríð, Eir, and Aurboða — the company Fjölsviðr names at Menglöð's knees. The Holy Place: Fjölsvinnsmál's promise: the maidens protect those who make offering at the sacred stead, and no sickness shall drag them down. The Superlative: Læknir beztr — 'the best physician': the only office Snorri gives her, and the only medical title in the ásynjur catalogue. Symbols: Lyfjaberg — The mountain of remedies — healing made landscape, the high place where help is found; The nine maidens — Protection, brightness, joy, mercy: the named company whose gifts are the inventory of recovery; The altar at the holy place — The covenant of Fjölsvinnsmál — sacrifice answered with deliverance from sickness; Menglöð's knee — The healing maidens sit at the necklace-glad one's knees — mercy attendant upon splendour; The name itself — Eir, 'help, mercy': the remedy and the plea for it in a single word Eir has the thinnest dossier of any goddess in the Edda — one superlative in Snorri's catalogue and one stanza-list in the Poetic Edda — and the office both witnesses agree on: she heals. Nothing else about her was ever written down. Gylfaginning 35: The Best Physician Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur runs like a court roll: Frigg is highest; second is Sága at Søkkvabekkr; and then, without genealogy, marriage, or adventure, the third entry: 'Eir is the third: she is the best physician' — Eir er þriðja: hon er læknir beztr. That is the whole notice. No hall is named, no parentage given, no deed narrated. In a catalogue that finds something to say about every goddess — Fulla's headband, Gefjun's plough, Syn's door-keeping — Eir alone is defined by a profession and a superlative, and the profession is medicine. Fjölsvinnsmál 38-40: The Maidens of Lyfjaberg The Poetic Edda keeps her second witness in the strangest of its love-quests. Svipdagr, come to win Menglöð, must answer the gate-ward Fjölsviðr riddle for riddle; among his questions is this: what are the maids called who sit at Menglöð's knees in harmony together? Fjölsviðr names nine: Hlíf the protectress, Hlífþursa, Þjóðvarta, Björt the bright, Blíð and Blíðr the blithe, Fríð the fair, Eir, and Aurboða. Then comes the promise that makes the list matter: these maidens will give help if men make offering at the holy place, and no sickness so cruel will seize the sons of men that they cannot free them from it. Menglöð's seat is Lyfjaberg, the mountain of healing — and Eir, 'mercy', stands named in its company. Skáldskaparmál þulur: Valkyrie and Kenning The name has a quieter afterlife in the poets' apparatus. The þulur — the metrical name-lists preserved with the Prose Edda — count an Eir among the valkyries, and the skalds used eir as a base-word in kennings for women, as the handbooks register: 'Eir of the ale' or 'Eir of rings' is simply a woman, any goddess's name being lawful tender in the kenning system. Whether the valkyrie Eir is the physician of Gylfaginning under another aspect or a second bearer of the name, the sources do not say; Simek registers the double attestation and leaves the door open. What the kennings prove is that the name lived in the working memory of the poets. Scholarly discussion: The Menglöð Question Who is the lady of Lyfjaberg whom Eir attends? Menglöð — 'the one gladdened by necklaces' — bears a name that points straight at Freyja, owner of the Brísingamen, and much scholarship has taken Menglöð as a byname or hypostasis of the Vanadís rather than a separate figure; the two poems of Svipdagsmál as a whole have often been read as a fragmentary Freyja-myth. The identification is attractive and unprovable, and the cautious handbooks present it as exactly that. If it holds, then the North's one physician sits in Freyja's own retinue — mercy among the attendants of love; if it does not, Lyfjaberg keeps its own mistress, and Eir keeps hers. Syncretism: No interpretatio romana ever found Eir a Latin name: the classical authors who mapped the northern gods left her unmentioned, and the medieval Icelandic writers who knew her wrote no equation. Her real company is native. The Germanic world knew healing as a craft guarded by female figures and spoken charms — the Second Merseburg Charm, the one surviving Old High German healing spell with divine names, binds Wodan and the healing of a wrenched foot in a formula that has Norse echoes, and the Edda's own Oddrúnargrátr gives a mortal woman, Oddrún, the role of birth-helper 'come from the southland'. Eir is the divine end of that continuum: the household of healing maidens on Lyfjaberg raised to the rank of ásynja. Modern comparisons with Greek healing deities are analogies of office, not borrowings — the name eir is transparently Norse, the common noun for mercy, and the tradition grew its physician out of its own vocabulary of help. Cultural legacy: Eir's afterlife is quiet and remarkably alive. The name never died in the North: Eir remains a living Icelandic given name, and its family survives in the everyday verb eira, 'to spare, to show mercy'. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice, which keeps few of the lesser ásynjur in regular use, has made room for her precisely because her office is the one every household needs — she is invoked in healing rites as the physician Snorri named. Popular culture reached her through the valkyrie list: an Eir numbered among the valkyries appears in modern games and fiction, usually in the healer's role the þulur and Gylfaginning between them suggest. Her scholarly afterlife is disproportionate to her dossier: the two-sentence goddess of Gylfaginning 35 is the standing proof, cited in every handbook, that the Norse pantheon contained an explicit deity of medicine. Extended meditation: Eir is the goddess made of a single word, and the word is mercy. The Edda gives her no story because her name is already the story: eir is what the wounded ask for and what the healer gives — help, clemency, the staying of a hand. Snorri places her third among the goddesses, ahead of figures with far longer dossiers, as if the catalogue itself understood that a pantheon without a physician would be incomplete. Fjölsvinnsmál completes the portrait by giving her a company and a mountain: mercy does not work alone but sits named among protection, brightness, gladness, and peace — the full inventory of what recovery feels like from the inside. To say her name in Old Norse was already to ask for the one thing medicine and prayer both promise. Original script note: The normalized Old Norse form is Eir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛅᛁᚱ (a-i-r, the ᛁ rune writing both e and i, ᚱ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: eir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

title: Hunter, Seer, Leader
text: Hunter, Seer, Leader: The Salmon of Knowledge, the Burning of Tara, and the Long Chase of the Fianna Fionn mac Cumhaill is the great captain of the Fianna, the war-band of young hunters and fighters who held the marches of Ireland between the king's peace and the wild: the boy who burned his thumb on the Salmon of Knowledge and swallowed all wisdom with it, the youth who saved Tara from fire on Samain night, and the aging leader who spent sixteen years pursuing Diarmaid and Gráinne across the country he had sworn to protect. The Salmon of Knowledge: An eo fis — the fish that fed on the nuts of the nine hazels over the well of Segais; whoever ate it would know all things. The Thumb of Knowledge: Burned on the salmon's blister and sucked by reflex — afterward Fionn could chew his thumb and the imbas, the great knowledge, would come. The Magic Spear: The birga Fíacha mac Conga put in his hand at Tara: held with its point to the forehead, its enchantment kept a man awake against Aillén's music. Bran and Sceólang: His two great hounds, born of his own transformed kin — the chase made family, and the Fianna's swiftest trackers. Symbols: The salmon of knowledge — Wisdom caught in a single instant — meant for another, given by chance, and never returned; The thumb — Imbas forosnai, the knowledge that illuminates — knowing held in the body, summoned by the bite; The magic spear — The discipline to stay awake when the whole court is lulled — vigilance as a weapon; The hounds Bran and Sceólang — The bond of hunter and hunted bound into one kinship — the wild running at the leader's heel; Ben Bulben — The boar's mountain in Sligo, where the long pursuit of Diarmaid ended and the water slipped through Fionn's fingers Fionn's cycle is the fullest hero-corpus Ireland kept: the Boyhood Deeds that make him wise, the Fenian lays and ballads that make him captain, and the two late romances — the pursuit of Diarmaid and the lay of Oisín — that make him tragic. Macgnímartha Finn: The Boy in the Wild Fionn's father was Cumhall mac Trénmhóir, captain of the Fianna, who abducted Muirne, daughter of the druid Tadg, when her father refused her. Tadg's appeal brought the king's army, and Cumhall fell at the battle of Cnucha to Goll mac Morna, head of the rival Clann Morna. Muirne bore the child in danger and gave him to two women to rear in secret: Bodbmall the druidess and Liath Luachra the warrior-woman, who raised him in the wild places away from his father's enemies. The boy they hid was named Demne; the name the world would keep was still swimming in the Boyne. Macgnímartha Finn: The Salmon of Knowledge Demne came to learn poetry from Finn Éces, Finn the poet, who had waited seven years on the Boyne for the salmon of knowledge — the fish that had fed on the nuts of the nine hazels dropping into the well of Segais, so that all the knowledge of the world was in its flesh. When at last the salmon was caught, the poet set the boy to cook it and forbade him to taste any part of it. A blister rose on the fish's skin; Demne pressed it down with his thumb, burned himself, and thrust the thumb into his mouth — and the knowledge was his. Finn Éces asked the boy his name, heard 'Demne', and told him: Finn is your name now, for it was Finn who was prophesied to eat this salmon. The boy ate what remained, and ever after needed only to chew his thumb to know what was hidden. Macgnímartha Finn: Aillén and the Burning of Tara Every Samain night for twenty-three years, Aillén of the three tongues came out of síd Finnachaidh and burned Tara: he played his timpán so sweetly that every man in the fortress fell asleep, and then he breathed fire over the hall. Fionn came to Tara on Samain, and Fíacha mac Conga, who had served his father, gave him a magic spear and the instruction: hold its naked point to your forehead, and you will not sleep. So Fionn sat wakeful while the court slept around him, and when Aillén turned back for the síd, Fionn cast the spear through him. For that deed Conn Cétchathach restored to him his father's treasure and made him head of the Fianna — and Goll mac Morna, his father's killer, accepted the peace and became the most loyal of his captains. Tóruigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghráinne: The Pursuit of Diarmaid and Gráinne In his age Fionn was betrothed to Gráinne, daughter of Cormac mac Airt, but at the feast she gave a sleeping-draught to the company and laid a geis — the bond no Fenian could refuse — on Diarmaid Ó Duibhne to take her away. Diarmaid bore a ball seirce, a love-spot on his forehead that no woman could see without loving him, and Gráinne had seen it. For sixteen years the Fianna hunted the pair the length of Ireland, with Óengus of the Brug shielding Diarmaid where he could, until the tale came to the boar-hunt on Ben Bulben: the beast was Diarmaid's own foster-brother, transformed, and it was fated to be his death. Diarmaid killed the boar and took its venom in the doing. Fionn could heal any wound with water carried in his two cupped hands — he had the gift since the salmon — and twice he brought the water from the well and let it slip through his fingers, remembering Gráinne; when Óscar's reproach sent him back the third time, Diarmaid was dead. Acallam na Senórach / Laoi Oisín: Oisín in Tír na nÓg and the Long Memory Fionn's son Oisín was taken across the sea by Niamh of the Golden Hair, daughter of the king of Tír na nÓg, the Land of Youth, riding behind her on a white horse that never touched water. What he counted as three years in that country were three hundred years in Ireland. Homesick, he was lent the horse to visit and warned on no account to set foot on Irish soil; he found the Fianna gone and their names become legend, and as he stooped from the saddle to help men shift a stone, the girth broke. Oisín touched the ground, and three hundred years fell on him at once. The medieval Acallam na Senórach frames the whole Fenian memory on this survival: the old, blind Oisín and Caílte mac Rónáin traveling Christian Ireland with Saint Patrick, naming every hill and ford and telling how they were won — the Fianna kept alive as long as one man could still remember them. Syncretism: Fionn's deepest kin are onomastic and Insular. His name descends from Proto-Celtic *windos, 'white, fair', and the handbooks have long set him beside the Welsh Gwyn ap Nudd — 'white son of Nudd', the Otherworld huntsman of Welsh tradition — as two regional developments of a Celtic figure built on the same word: the fair one who rides between this world and the wild. The more famous comparison is with the Norse corpus: like Sigurðr, who tasted the blood of Fáfnir's heart and understood the speech of birds, Fionn receives a whole mode of knowledge through a single accidental taste — the parallel is a commonplace of the comparative literature, though the two traditions grew the motif independently. Within Ireland his nearest mirror is [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], the Ulster Cycle's solitary champion set against Fionn's communal war-band: the two heroes divide the Irish heroic imagination between them. Cultural legacy: Fionn became, for a century, the most famous Celt in Europe. James Macpherson's Fragments of Ancient Poetry (1760) and Fingal (1762) presented 'Ossian' — Oisín — as the bard of a northern Homer, with Fingal his mighty father; the poems swept the continent, were carried by Napoleon and quoted by Goethe, and set off a running war over their authenticity in which Samuel Johnson demanded the manuscripts and Macpherson never produced them. The Celtic Revival reclaimed the genuine cycle: Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) brought the Fenian tales into modern English, and Irish scholarship — Meyer's Fianaigecht, Murphy's Duanaire Finn, Dooley and Roe's Acallam translation — rebuilt the cycle from its real witnesses. In Ireland the name never faded: Fianna Éireann named the warrior-band after him, the political tradition borrowed Fianna Fáil, 'the war-band of Ireland', Finn is once again a living given name, and Tír na nÓg remains the Irish idiom for youth that outlasts its bargain. Extended meditation: Fionn is the patron of accidental wisdom — of the knowledge you were not supposed to have, caught while doing someone else's cooking. The salmon was seven years promised to Finn Éces, and it went to the kitchen-boy's burned thumb instead; the tradition does not call this theft, and it does not pretend the boy planned it. It says something harder: that readiness is the only part of fortune you can control. The rest of Fionn's life is the price and use of that gift — the long captaincy, the saved Tara, the sixteen-year pursuit in which knowledge and desire pulled opposite ways and he let the water fall. The Acallam gives him the last word through his son: wisdom is memory kept against time, and it survives only as long as somebody keeps telling it. Original script note: The normalized Irish form is Fionn — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of Find or any Fenian name has been read on them.
